kept.title: Quick Share announcement never registers: mdns-sd 0.21 refuses the hostname, so no Android phone can ever see Sukkula as a receiver (F-QS1, F-QS4)
kept.rule: F-QS1
kept.description: build_service passes the bare instance name (14 base64url characters, no domain) as ServiceInfo's host_name. That worked on the mdns-sd 0.10.4 fork upstream used. Patch 0007 moved to crates.io mdns-sd 0.21.4, and since 0.11.0 its ServiceDaemon::register() calls check_hostname(), which rejects any hostname that does not end in ".local." (mdns-sd-0.21.4 src/service_daemon.rs:539-541 and 4712-4714). normalize_hostname (service_info.rs:544-550) only strips a doubled ".local." and never adds one. So MDnsServer::run (mdns.rs:58, `self.daemon.register(...)?`) returns Err before its loop, and nothing is ever announced. The engine logs this at debug only (crates/sukkula-engine/src/quickshare/receive.rs:79-81) while start_receiving reports success. The failure is invisible in CI because every Quick Share test sets `mdns: false` (tests/quickshare.rs:209, quickshare_ble.rs:503, s9_logs.rs:571), and nothing ever calls register.
kept.failure_scenario: Turn on Receive with the default visibility, Everyone. receive::start spawns MDnsServer::run, register() returns Err("Hostname must end with '.local.': <name>"), and the task ends. The TCP listener runs, but no PTR/SRV/TXT/A record is ever published. A Pixel or Samsung share sheet never lists the phone, so Quick Share receiving over the LAN does not work at all. Everyone behaves like Hidden, so M-30 fails and M-33 passes for the wrong reason.
kept.suggested_fix: Give the service a valid host name, e.g. `&format!("{name}.local.")`. Make start_receiving fail, or at least warn, when register() errors. Add a test that runs MDnsServer on loopback and resolves the service with a second daemon.

kept.title: mdns-sd caches every record from every LAN host with no limit, and grows its timer heap per packet: remote memory exhaustion
kept.rule: S4/S6, 'no memory exhaustion from any input'
kept.description: R12's fix bounds only rqs_lib's own 64-entry map. The mdns-sd 0.21.4 daemon under it (MDnsDiscovery here, and MDnsServer at mdns.rs:41 once the registration above works) has no bound of its own. In handle_response, `is_for_us` starts true and only a PTR answer for an unbrowsed type makes it false (service_daemon.rs:3095-3121). A response carrying only SRV/TXT/A records is therefore taken whole: every record in all sections goes into DnsCache (service_daemon.rs:3144-3190; dns_cache.rs:249-307 has no size cap, only TTL expiry, and the TTL is the sender's u32). Every added or refreshed record also pushes two entries onto the timers BinaryHeap (service_daemon.rs:3187-3189, 1820-1822). The socket is bound to 0.0.0.0:5353 and accepts unicast packets too, and nothing checks the source address or port of a response.
kept.failure_scenario: While the user is on the send page (discovery running), a host on the Wi-Fi sends datagrams of about 8.9 KB to 224.0.0.251:5353 or to the phone's IP:5353. Each is a response with about 440 A records for fresh names (x1.local., x2.local., ...) at TTL 0xFFFFFFFF. Each record costs a heap-allocated record, a name String and a map entry: roughly ten times its wire size, kept indefinitely. Re-sending one fixed set instead grows the timer heap by 16 bytes per record per packet. The timer-driven eviction scans (service_daemon.rs:1644-1658) also get linearly slower. The Sukkula process grows at LAN speed until it is OOM-killed. There is no consent and no rate limit, and rqs_lib's MAX_DISCOVERED_ENDPOINTS does not help.
kept.suggested_fix: Carry a patch to mdns-sd, like rqs_lib's, that caps cache entries per type and in total, drops records not for a queried name or type, caps TTLs, and does not re-push timers on refresh. Alternatively, browse with a small bounded parser of our own. Add a hostile-response test with a memory assertion.

kept.title: Progress throttle is skipped once bytes >= total, so a Quick Share peer can flood the UI with events after acceptance
kept.rule: S6 / bounded resource use (SECURITY.md 'crash, hang, or unbounded ... CPU use triggered by a peer')
kept.description: TransferHandle::add_progress is meant to report at most every 250 ms, but its condition is `last.is_none_or(elapsed >= PROGRESS_INTERVAL) || bytes >= self.total`. Once the counter reaches the total, every call emits a TransferProgress event with no throttle, and that includes zero-length chunks. ReceivingFile::write (ctx.rs:324-332) accepts a zero-length chunk and calls add_progress(0) every time. Nothing in the shared receive path limits empty chunks. The wormhole adapter works around this itself (MAX_EMPTY_RECORDS in wormhole/receive.rs), which shows the problem is known, but ctx does not enforce it. The Quick Share adapter passes every FileChunk body straight to incoming.write (quickshare/receive.rs:379). The patched rqs_lib accepts an empty non-last chunk as long as its offset matches (third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/inbound.rs:615-654). Each frame restarts the idle timeout, so this can go on indefinitely.
kept.failure_scenario: A LAN peer offers one 0-byte file over Quick Share, or one N-byte file whose N bytes it sends with the `last` flag clear. The user accepts. The peer then streams PayloadTransfer File frames with an empty body, the correct offset and last=false, as fast as the LAN allows. For every frame, bytes >= total holds (0 >= 0, or N >= N), so ctx emits a TransferProgress. That means one JSON event per frame, tens of thousands per second, sustained until the user manages to press Cancel. The event gate's backpressure blocks the tokio worker running the task in a Condvar wait (hub.rs push), and the C++ bridge keeps the GUI thread saturated up to MaxUndelivered. Two such transfers stall both engine workers. KeepAlive and the transfer slot are held the whole time.
kept.suggested_fix: Emit the final report once, for example by storing the last reported byte count and skipping the report when nothing changed (`bytes == last_bytes`). Also, return early from add_progress when n == 0, or refuse or count empty chunks in ReceivingFile::write, so no adapter can drive the event path with zero-byte writes.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this. Every step of the claim matches the code.

1. The throttle bypass is real. In `TransferHandle::add_progress` (crates/sukkula-engine/src/ctx.rs:510-529) the condition is `last.is_none_or(elapsed >= 250ms) || bytes >= self.total`. The code never records the last byte count it reported, and `n == 0` does not return early. Once `bytes >= total`, every call emits `Event::TransferProgress`. `total` is the sum of the offered file sizes (ctx.rs:390), so a single-file transfer reaches it as soon as the declared bytes have arrived.

2. Zero-length writes get through the shared path.
   - `ReceivingFile::write` (ctx.rs:324-332) only checks for cancellation. It then calls `Incoming::write` and `add_progress(chunk.len())`.
   - `sukkula_core::inbox::Incoming::write` (inbox.rs:310-334) accepts an empty chunk whenever `written + 0 <= declared`, including when `written == declared`.
   - tokio's `write_all` on an empty slice returns immediately, so each empty chunk costs almost nothing and does not yield.

3. The Quick Share path lets these chunks through.
   - Patched rqs_lib (third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/inbound.rs:~590-650) checks only that the offset matches, that `after <= total`, and that a chunk with `last` set ends exactly at the declared size. An empty chunk with `last=false` at offset == total passes and yields `InboundEvent::FileChunk`.
   - The adapter loop (quickshare/receive.rs:330-395) calls `incoming.write(&chunk.body)` and only commits and removes the file from `pending` when `chunk.last` is set. The loop therefore keeps going.
   - Each frame restarts the idle timeout, and there is no per-connection frame, empty-chunk or rate limit. `frame.rs` refuses zero-length frames, but a PayloadTransfer frame with an empty body is not a zero-length frame.
   - The wormhole receiver does guard against this (`MAX_EMPTY_RECORDS = 16`, and its loop ends at `remaining() == 0`). Quick Share has no equivalent, and the ctx layer has none either.

4. The consequence is real and breaks a documented contract.
   - docs/FFI.md says `transfer_progress` is sent "At most four times a second per transfer". This bug lets a peer send one per frame.
   - The event closure is `Gate::emit` (hub.rs:210-215). When 1024 events are queued, `Gate::push` blocks the calling tokio worker in a Condvar (hub.rs:1005-1020). The runtime has only 2 workers (hub.rs:227). The C++ bridge also blocks at `MaxUndelivered = 256` (bridge.cpp:155), so the engine is throttled only by how fast the GUI can drain events.
   - Memory stays bounded. CPU does not: the GUI thread and the engine workers stay saturated for as long as the peer keeps sending. SECURITY.md lists "unbounded ... CPU use triggered by a peer" as in scope.

5. Nothing mitigates it. No earlier check stops empty non-last chunks, and no existing test covers them. The only way out is user action: pressing Cancel, which is slowed down because the workers are mostly blocked and the GUI is flooded (the cancel still gets through when tokio makes the task yield), or turning Receive off.

Why medium rather than higher: the peer only gets this far after the user accepts its offer. Memory does not grow, nothing crashes, and the user can end it with Cancel or by turning Receive off. It is still an in-scope, peer-triggered CPU denial of service that runs indefinitely and breaks the documented rate contract, so medium stands.

The suggested fix is sound. Track the last reported byte count and skip the report when nothing changed, or return early on `n == 0`. Separately, counting or refusing empty chunks in the shared path (or in the Quick Share adapter, like wormhole's `MAX_EMPTY_RECORDS`) would also stop the indefinite keep-alive.

2. **Nothing refuses a zero-length write.**

3. **Quick Share passes empty chunks through.**

   - `read_frame` / `process_frame` have no frame-rate or frame-count limit.
   - Every frame restarts the `idle` timeout in the receive loop, and the loop has no overall deadline.

4. **Nothing downstream merges the events.**
   - `Gate::push` in `hub.rs` (around lines 1005-1036) is a plain bounded FIFO: 1024 events or 4 MiB. When it is full, the emitting thread blocks on a `Condvar`, and the runtime has `worker_threads(2)`.
   - `src/bridge.cpp` blocks at `MaxUndelivered = 256` and posts each event to the GUI thread.
   - `Engine.qml` `_onTransferProgress` handles each event by doing `setProperty`, `_recount()` and `transferUpdated`.

5. **It breaks a documented promise.** `docs/FFI.md:398` says `transfer_progress` arrives "At most four times a second per transfer". A peer can break that without limit.

6. **The project already guards this vector elsewhere.** The wormhole adapter caps empty records itself (`MAX_EMPTY_RECORDS = 16`, "No reference client sends any"). The shared ctx path and the Quick Share adapter have no equivalent guard.

**Severity: medium.** Memory stays bounded because both queues are capped. Nothing crashes. The attack also needs the user to have accepted the offer, and the user can still cancel. A peer can already make the engine spend CPU on every frame, for example with KeepAlive frames. What this bug adds is turning each tiny frame into a GUI-thread event, sustained indefinitely, while engine workers sit blocked on backpressure. That is the "unbounded CPU use triggered by a peer" that `docs/SECURITY.md` puts in scope, and it breaks the FFI rate guarantee. If you weigh the consent requirement and the Cancel escape heavily, low would also be defensible.

kept.title: A client that pipelines requests and stops reading holds a server connection forever; 4 LAN addresses take all 32 slots
kept.rule: S6 / SECURITY.md 'hang ... triggered by a peer' / module doc L3
kept.description: `serve` puts a timeout on the TLS handshake (line 341). After that it relies on hyper's `header_read_timeout` (line 367). The select loop at 375-394 ends only when the connection completes, the engine stops, the server is closing, or a drain happens. It has no timer for a connection that makes no progress. In hyper 1.11.1 the header timer is armed only inside `Conn::poll_read_head`, and the dispatcher only gets there when `Server::poll_ready` sees no request in flight. That check stays Pending while a response is waiting to be flushed (dispatch.rs 301-311, 634-640; conn.rs 211-233). tokio-rustls buffers at most 64 KiB of plaintext and then returns Pending. There is no write timeout and no TCP_USER_TIMEOUT. Linux keeps probing a zero window for as long as the peer ACKs the probes. So once a peer stops reading, nothing on the connection ever times out again. This is the reverse (slow-read) case of the slow-loris attack L3 claims to fix, and the hostile suite does not cover it.
kept.failure_scenario: From one permitted LAN address, open 8 TLS connections (any self-signed client cert passes `AnySelfSigned`). On each, set a tiny SO_RCVBUF, write about 2,000 pipelined `GET /x HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n` requests (an unknown path returns 404 and is not rate-limited; about 40 KB in all), and never read. The roughly 270 KB of 404 replies fill the kernel send buffer, rustls's 64 KiB buffer and hyper's write buffer. hyper stops parsing heads, and no timer is ever armed. Do the same from 3 more addresses: all MAX_CONNECTIONS=32 permits are held, and `try_acquire_owned` (line 315) drops every honest sender's connection for as long as the attacker likes. Only switching Receive off (drain) frees them, and the attacker reconnects at once.
kept.suggested_fix: Put a bound on a connection that stops making progress. For example, wrap the TCP/TLS stream in an IO adapter that fails any read or write pending longer than idle_timeout, or set TCP_USER_TIMEOUT through socket2 (safe API). Also cap requests per keep-alive connection, or set an overall deadline for connections that are not carrying the active session's upload. Add a hostile test that pipelines requests and never reads.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this. I checked the code, read hyper's source and reproduced the hang.

**Code** (crates/sukkula-engine/src/localsend/server.rs, lines 332-395):
- `serve` puts a timeout only on the TLS accept.
- After that it relies on hyper's `header_read_timeout(handshake)`.
- The select loop ends only on: the connection finishing, `stop`, `closing` (bounded by a sleep only after `closing`), or `drain`.
- Nothing wraps the IO, there is no write deadline, no TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and no socket keepalive; the only socket option set is `set_nodelay`.
- Nothing elsewhere in the engine limits how long a server connection lives.

**hyper 1.11.1** (from Cargo.lock):
- The header timer is armed only in `Conn::poll_read_head` (conn.rs ~212-233). That is reached only when `can_read_head()` is true, which needs `reading == Init`.
- A request with no body leaves `reading = KeepAlive` (conn.rs ~301). It goes back to `Init` only through `try_keep_alive`.
- The write path calls `try_keep_alive` only after `poll_flush` succeeds (conn.rs 838-842).
- So once the flush is stuck, `poll_read` goes to `poll_read_keep_alive`, then `mid_message_detect_eof`. That returns Pending: straight away if pipelined bytes are still buffered, otherwise on a read that never finishes. No timer is armed.
- tokio-rustls 0.26.5 `poll_write_vectored` returns Pending, not `Ok(0)`, when rustls's buffer is full and the socket blocks. So hyper waits; it does not fail with WriteZero.
- One detail differs from the claim: `Server::poll_ready` does not stay Pending, because `in_flight` clears when the service future finishes. The mechanism is still the same: the connection stays stuck in the reading=KeepAlive/writing=KeepAlive state waiting on the flush, with no timer running.

**Reproduction.** I built a scratch crate outside the repo, with hyper =1.11.1, hyper-util =0.1.21, tokio =1.53.1 and the same builder settings (timer, `header_read_timeout` 2 s, `max_buf_size` 64 KiB, `max_headers` 32, keep_alive), over plain TCP; TLS only adds a buffer. Each 404 reply was 138 bytes.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1 request, client reads | connection ends at 2.0 s ("read header from client timeout") |
| 20,000 pipelined requests, client reads | ends at 2.85 s |
| 20,000 pipelined requests, SO_RCVBUF 1 KiB, client never reads | still open after 15 s (outer timeout hit) |

The Linux kernel keeps probing a zero window for as long as the peer answers the probes, unless TCP_USER_TIMEOUT is set. That makes the hold indefinite.

**Tests.** The hostile suite covers slow handshakes, slow heads and slow bodies, and a *receiver* that stops reading (our client side). It has no server-side test where the peer stops reading.

**Rules.** This breaks SECURITY.md's "hang ... triggered by a peer" and its table row "slow peers are cut off". It also defeats the protection claimed in the module doc (L3). A LAN attacker needs a self-signed certificate, which `AnySelfSigned` accepts, and 4 addresses × 8 connections to fill all `MAX_CONNECTIONS` (32). After that, `try_acquire_owned` refuses every honest connection. It is not one of the listed known limitations; only the two consent slots are.

**Severity: medium.** This is only a denial of service of LocalSend receive by someone on the LAN, with no data impact. The total number of descriptors stays capped at 32. Turning Receive off frees the connections, but the attacker can take them again once Receive is back on. An attacker who keeps reconnecting could already fill the slots with ordinary slow-loris connections, each held up to about 40 s (20 s handshake plus 20 s header timeout). This bug adds a hold that needs no further traffic and never ends, and it breaks a guarantee the project states. That keeps it at medium rather than high.

kept.title: Opening the consent dialog over Settings saves the settings and restarts receivers, which cancels the offer being shown
kept.rule: F-C2 / F-LS4
kept.description: SettingsPage runs save() on every change to PageStatus.Deactivating, not only when the user leaves the page. The page goes Deactivating whenever anything is pushed on top of it. harbour-sukkula.qml navigate() pushes the ConsentDialog over whatever page is showing (line 76), so an incoming offer also triggers save(). If any field differs from engine.settings, save() sends set_settings. In the engine (hub.rs SetSettings), receiving being on means restart_receiving(), which calls stop_receiving on every adapter. For LocalSend, stop_receiving calls server.drain(), and drain() cancels a Slot::Pending (localsend/server.rs:261), which is exactly the connection whose offer the dialog is showing. The save also commits whatever the user has typed so far, even though they never left the page.
kept.failure_scenario: Receive is on. The user opens Settings and renames the phone so a friend can find it, or toggles Debug logging, or starts typing a new PIN ("73" of "7342"). The friend's LocalSend or Quick Share offer arrives. ConsentDialog is pushed, SettingsPage goes Deactivating, save() sends set_settings, the receivers restart and the pending LocalSend slot is cancelled. offer_closed arrives, the dialog closes itself (closedByEngine) before the user can tap anything, and the sender is refused. Meanwhile the partial PIN "73" (or a half-typed ws:// mailbox URL) becomes the live setting.
kept.suggested_fix: Save only on back navigation away from the page (for example, check that the page is no longer in the stack, or save from Component.onDestruction or a pop), not on every Deactivating. Alternatively, skip the save when the page stack's new top page is the consent dialog.

I could not refute it. I traced the whole chain and each step holds.

Nothing checks whether the page is actually being left. save() has four guards, and none of them stops this case: loaded, valid, settingsKnown, and "changed vs engine.settings". The header comment says "saved when the page is left", and tst_settings.qml says "saved on the way out". So saving because something was pushed on top is not the intended design.

2. Deactivating on a push. When a page is pushed, the page underneath goes Deactivating, both in real Silica and in the repo's own stub (qml-stubs/Sailfish/Silica/PageStack.qml, push() then _hide(currentPage) sets Deactivating). In qml/harbour-sukkula.qml, navigate() pushes pages/ConsentDialog.qml over whatever is showing on onOfferArrived. It only checks pageStack.busy and consentPage === null, and nothing excludes SettingsPage.

For LocalSend, localsend/mod.rs:677 calls server.drain(), and localsend/server.rs:254-272 cancels a Slot::Pending's token. In prepare_upload (server.rs:~515), the select on pending.cancel.cancelled() then drops the shared.ctx.offer(raw) future and answers 403 "Cancelled". Dropping that future runs Waiting::drop in sukkula-core/src/consent.rs:~270. That emits ConsentEvent::Closed{Withdrawn}, which hub.rs:762 turns into offer_closed. ConsentDialog then sets closedByEngine and closes itself. Quick Share's stop_receiving also tears down the running receiver.

So the scenario can happen as described. Receive is on, the user has unsaved edits in Settings, and an offer arrives. The dialog is pushed and settings are saved mid-edit. The receivers restart and the offer is withdrawn before the user can answer. The sender gets refused.

Why medium rather than higher: it fails closed. Nothing is accepted without consent. The partial PIN or URL stays live only until the user leaves the page, which saves again. The sender can retry. It still breaks the consent flow (F-C2) and commits settings the user never confirmed. The trigger is also more likely than random timing: people often open Settings (rename, PIN, visibility) exactly while a friend is trying to send. The same premature save also happens when About is pushed from the pull-down menu.

kept.title: Discovery peer tables fill first-come with no per-source cap, and one per-IP budget keyed on spoofable or attacker-chosen addresses also gates TLS-proven /register; no flood-then-honest test
kept.rule: S7; clove evil-peer contract (a misbehaving peer cannot deny service to an honest one)
kept.description:
clove shows the practice in /home/user/muhnschein/clove/crates/clove-core/tests/evil_peer.rs. `one_destination_cannot_monopolise_the_peer_table` (line 1664) and `a_pex_flood_cannot_shut_out_the_trackers_peers` (line 1744) check that one source cannot fill the peer table and that entries from a weaker source cannot shut out better-proven ones. Every scenario there ends with an honest peer getting through, and clove's SECURITY.md lists both as guarantees.

Sukkula has none of this. When the Quick Share peer table is full (quickshare/discovery.rs:160) it refuses every newcomer, and so do rqs_lib's own 64-entry mDNS cache (third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns_discovery.rs:93-96) and the LocalSend table (localsend/peers.rs:82, where the module comment chooses 'not admitted until a stale one expires'). None of the three limits entries per source.

Quick Share takes a peer's address from the A record the announcer wrote, not from the packet source (mdns_discovery.rs:105-133). That same address is also the rate-limit key (quickshare/discovery.rs:128).

One `Ctx::discovery_limiter` (ctx.rs:171) serves every discovery input. Some of those inputs are unauthenticated: the LocalSend multicast `screen` with its spoofable UDP source (localsend/discovery.rs:179), and the Quick Share mDNS A record. Others are TLS-proven: LocalSend `/info` and `/register` (server.rs:438, 448).

The test `peers_are_bounded_and_reported` (tests/quickshare.rs:544-563) fills all 64 slots from a single address and asserts that as correct. No test floods discovery and then requires an honest peer to be listed.
kept.failure_scenario:
Filling the table: one LAN host answers the Quick Share browse with 64 mDNS services, each with a distinct instance name and an A record from 192.168.1.10 to .73. It needs no IP spoofing, and each fake address is permitted and gets its own rate bucket. The host re-announces within the TTL. rqs_lib's cache and Sukkula's table are now full. A real Android phone's announcement is dropped at `cache.len() >= MAX_DISCOVERED_ENDPOINTS` or `by_id.len() >= MAX_PEERS` and is never listed while the attacker keeps refreshing. For LocalSend, one address can register 64 self-made certificates within 80 s (8 per 10 s) and hold them; any peer that appears later is refused.

Draining one victim: about one announcement per 1.25 s names the victim laptop's IP, either as an mDNS A record or as the spoofed UDP source of a LocalSend multicast datagram with a random fingerprint. That keeps `allow_discovery(victim_ip)` at zero. The laptop's own TLS `POST /register` then gets 429, and its announcements are screened out, so it never appears on the Send page for either protocol.

With the honest peers suppressed, the only entries named like the user's own devices are the attacker's, so a tap sends the user's files to the attacker.
kept.suggested_fix: Cap entries per packet-source address in both tables and in rqs_lib's cache. Key Quick Share on the packet source, not on the announced A record. Evict unproven multicast/mDNS-only entries before TLS-proven ones. Give spoofable UDP inputs a budget separate from `/register` and `/info`. Add clove-style tests that flood discovery and then require an honest peer to be listed.

I looked for a check that would stop each step of the claim and found none. Every mechanism it describes is in the code.

1) Quick Share table fill (confirmed). In third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns_discovery.rs:93-96, the cache drops any new fullname once it holds 64 entries. It removes an entry only on ServiceRemoved, which comes from a goodbye or a TTL expiry, and an attacker who keeps refreshing never triggers either. Before a service is cached, the only checks are the reach filter on the announced A record (any private address passes), is_not_self_ip, and a parseable "n" TXT. None of them limits entries per source. The cache is filled before Sukkula's allow_discovery ever runs, so one LAN host with 64 instance names fills it even if all 64 use its own address. rqs_lib then never forwards a later honest phone. quickshare/discovery.rs:160 is also first-come and never evicts. Both are cleared only when discovery restarts (start() drains by_id, and run() builds a new cache). The attacker can answer the browse query at once, while an Android phone starts advertising only after the BLE nudge, so the attacker wins the race in practice. docs/UPSTREAM-QUICKSHARE.md R12 lists "stall discovery" by any host on the link as an impact to fix. The bounded first-come cache brings that stall back.

2) One shared per-IP budget (confirmed). hub.rs:719-728 gives every adapter the same Arc<Ctx>. Ctx::allow_discovery (ctx.rs:170-171) uses one limiter, 8 per 10 s per address, and all of these call it:
- quickshare/discovery.rs:128, keyed on the announced A record (the attacker chooses it; no spoofing needed)
- localsend/discovery.rs:179, keyed on the UDP source of the multicast datagram (spoofable)
- server.rs:438 (/info) and server.rs:448 (/register), both TLS-proven

mdns-sd 0.21.4 emits ServiceResolved again whenever an instance's records change (resolve_updated_instances). An attacker who alternates TXT or SRV values under a cached fullname whose A record is the victim's address therefore spends the victim's tokens without spoofing anything. So do spoofed-source LocalSend datagrams: screen() takes the token before the MAX_ANSWERS permit is checked. After that, the victim's POST /register gets 429, its multicast announcements fail screen(), and its real Quick Share ServiceResolved is dropped at line 128. That event is not retried, so the phone stays hidden for the whole round. To keep the bucket at zero, the attacker has to send faster than the claimed 1.25 s: the fixed-window refill happens on the first call after the window ends. Sending at a high rate is cheap, so the attack still works.

3) LocalSend table (confirmed, but weaker than claimed). peers.rs:82 is first-come with no per-source cap, and one address can add 8 fresh certificates per 10 s and keep them refreshed within the 100 s PEER_TTL. However, stop_discovery calls clear_peers and saw_peer runs only while discovering. Honest peers that answer our announcement when discovery starts are therefore listed before one address can fill 64 slots; only peers that arrive later are refused. The module comment also chooses this behaviour deliberately.

4) Tests (confirmed). peers_are_bounded_and_reported (tests/quickshare.rs:544-563) calls insert_peer 64 times from one address and asserts that the table is bounded. announcements_are_rate_limited_per_address only checks the per-address budget. No test floods discovery and then requires an honest peer to appear.

On the spec: S7 as literally written ("discovery replies are rate-limited per IP") is met, and discovery availability is not in SECURITY.md's explicit in-scope list. But the project holds itself to a no-denial-of-service standard in several places: localsend_hostile.rs contract 4 ("a hostile peer cannot deny service to an honest one"), SECURITY.md's comparison with clove (flood suites), and R12's treatment of stalled discovery as an impact. Neither discovery DoS nor the cross-protocol drain is recorded as a known limitation, while the similar consent-slot DoS is. So this is a real defect, not a documented choice, except for the LocalSend first-come rule, which is documented.

Severity stays at medium, not higher. It is a LAN denial of service with no write, crash or consent bypass. The final step, "files go to the attacker", still needs the user to tap an entry whose name the attacker chose, and these protocols never authenticate names anyway. Not lower either: the Quick Share lockout is trivial and complete from one unprivileged host, and an unauthenticated A record can starve a TLS-proven path for any chosen address.

A related issue I noticed but did not verify: Quick Share peers are keyed only by the endpoint id in the instance name, so an announcement reusing an honest phone's endpoint id with a different A record would overwrite that entry's address in by_id.

The code does what the claim says, but the claimed guarantee is not one Sukkula makes, so under the spec this is not a defect.

**The mechanics check out.** Every cited line matches the code:
- `quickshare/discovery.rs:160`, rqs_lib `mdns_discovery.rs:93-96` and `localsend/peers.rs:82` all fill first-come and turn newcomers away once they hold 64 entries.
- Quick Share keys the rate limit on the address in the announced A record (`discovery.rs:128`, fed from `mdns_discovery.rs:105-133`).
- The hub builds one `Ctx` (`hub.rs:221`), so a single `discovery_limiter` covers the LocalSend multicast `screen` (`localsend/discovery.rs:179`), `/info` and `/register` (`server.rs:438`, `server.rs:448`) and Quick Share mDNS.
- `peers_are_bounded_and_reported` fills the table from one address and asserts that result.
- One address can hold 64 LocalSend certificates: refreshing them takes 6.4 per 10 s, under the budget of 8 per 10 s (`DISCOVERY_BURST`), and the multicast answer path allows one port per certificate.

**Why it is refuted:**

1. **Out of scope under the spec.** SPEC §5 lists the security goals: nothing written outside the inbox, nothing accepted without consent, no crash or memory exhaustion, and no UI spoofing. Keeping discovery available is not among them.
   - S7 asks only for private-range reach and "discovery replies are rate-limited per IP", and the code does exactly that.
   - SECURITY.md's in-scope list covers crashes, hangs and unbounded memory, CPU or descriptor use. This attack stays bounded by design ("Bounded everything ... peers ... have hard caps").
   - "A misbehaving peer cannot deny service to an honest one" is clove's guarantee. Sukkula's SECURITY.md lists what it shares with clove, and this is not on that list. clove can cap per destination because its I2P destinations are cryptographic identities, which LAN addresses are not.

2. **LocalSend's first-come table is a documented choice.** The `peers.rs` module doc says a full table admits no one new until an entry expires, because "evicting on arrival would let a flood of fresh certificates push out the phone the user is about to send to". The claim asks to reverse a trade-off the authors wrote down on purpose.

3. **The attacker in the draining scenario could do the same by other means.** Draining one victim needs the attacker to spoof IP sources on the same Wi-Fi. That attacker, who is the spec's attacker, can also ARP-poison the victim's address or flood multicast, and so knock the victim off discovery (and more) whatever the app does.
   - The suggested per-source caps do not deliver the guarantee on a LAN either. The claim itself relies on spoofed UDP and mDNS sources, and a single host can take several addresses. mdns-sd's resolved-service info does not carry the packet source, so keying Quick Share on it would first need a library patch.

4. **The misdirected-send ending is an out-of-scope protocol weakness.** It depends on the attacker naming an entry like the user's device and the user tapping it. Anyone can announce such a name whether or not the table is full, and unauthenticated names are a weakness of the protocols themselves, which SECURITY.md puts out of scope. F-LS3 still holds: a send reaches only the fingerprint that was announced, and only after the user taps it.

**If kept anyway:** it is at most a low-severity hardening or documentation item. The most useful step would be to list "discovery tables can be filled or suppressed by a LAN attacker" under SECURITY.md's Known limitations, next to the consent-slot entry.

kept.title: Global offer budget is shared with user-initiated wormhole receives: a LAN attacker can make every wormhole receive fail as 'busy' and waste the code

kept.description: decide() takes a token from the single global_offer_limiter (10 per 60 s) for every well-formed offer from any protocol, before consent.ask. kept.failure_scenario: An attacker on the Wi-Fi uses 4 or more ULA or link-local source addresses (3 offers per minute each pass allow_offer). Right after each refill of the global bucket it sends 10 well-formed LocalSend prepare-upload requests and closes each connection at once (dialogs flash and are withdrawn). The user types a wormhole code, the PAKE succeeds, the offer arrives, ctx.offer returns Declined::Busy without any dialog, the sender sees 'transfer rejected', and the code is used up. kept.suggested_fix: Apply the global limiter only to unsolicited LAN offers: keep the check but skip it for Protocol::Wormhole, or move it into allow_offer. Consider spending the token only after consent.ask has actually queued the offer (after the pending-slot check).

kept.title: resume()/release() race closes the listener while Receive is reported on
kept.rule: F-C1
kept.description: `start_receiving` (mod.rs:658) checks `server.stopped()`, then calls `resume()`. `resume()` (245-248) replaces the drain token and only then stores `accepting=true`. - no data is lost;

kept.title: Forged UDP announcements spend a victim's shared discovery budget and hide it (also from Quick Share)
kept.rule: S7 (rate limit per IP) / F-LS1
kept.description: `screen` charges `ctx.allow_discovery(ip)` to the UDP source address of an announcement, and that address is unauthenticated and trivially forged. The same `discovery_limiter` (ctx.rs:170, 8 per 10 s) also gates authenticated TCP requests: `GET /info` and `POST /register` (server.rs:438, 448). The payload is well formed: `{"alias":"x","version":"2.2","fingerprint":"<any 64 hex>","port":53317,"protocol":"https"}`. Each passes `permits` and `answerable` and takes one of V's 8 tokens. V's real announcements are then dropped, and V's register reply to our announcement gets 429 (server.rs:448-450). V never appears in the Send list for LocalSend, and the same budget keeps V out of Quick Share discovery. Each forged datagram also makes us open a TLS connection to V pinned to a junk fingerprint (up to 4 at a time). The attacker needs no TCP connection and no address of its own.
kept.suggested_fix: Keep a separate budget for unauthenticated UDP sources, and never let it drain the per-IP budget that TCP requests (register/info, Quick Share) are held to. Alternatively, charge UDP-triggered answers to a small global budget.

  - V's real announcements are dropped in `screen`.

  - Quick Share events that resolve to V are dropped.

The extra TLS connections to V are capped at 8 per 10 s and 4 at a time, so that side effect is minor.

kept.rule: SECURITY.md known limitation: 'up to three outbound TCP connections to addresses it names'
kept.description: targets() limits the peer to three targets (their relay plus direct hints, truncated to MAX_TARGETS=4 with ours first). But the peer relay target keeps up to MAX_RELAY_ENDPOINTS=3 endpoints (wire.rs:42), and TransitGuard::connect tries every endpoint in turn, with up to MAX_ADDRS_PER_HOST=4 resolved addresses each, until one accepts. That is up to 12 TCP connection attempts to IP:port pairs the peer picks (IP literals are accepted as relay hosts, wire.rs:283), plus 2 direct hints. The relay line goes to the first address that answers. The only filter is peer_may_name, which blocks loopback, unspecified and multicast. Despite its comment 'Never our own machine', it does not block the phone's own interface addresses, which reach the phone's own services bound to 0.0.0.0.
kept.failure_scenario: After the user accepts a file, a sender holding the code sends the hint {"type":"relay-v1","hints":[{"type":"direct-tcp-v1","hostname":"192.168.1.1","port":22},{..."port":80},{..."port":443}]} and a name that resolves to four more internal hosts. The phone connects to each in turn: a probe of internal LAN services from the victim's phone, well past the stated bound, sending the relay line to whichever answers first.
kept.suggested_fix: Count connection attempts, not targets. Keep one endpoint (or one resolved address) per peer relay, or cap total peer-named connect() calls per transfer at the documented three. Also refuse the host's own interface addresses, or fix the comment and SECURITY.md.

votes.reasoning:
The claim's description of the code is accurate. The problem is smaller than the failure scenario says.

Checked in the code:
- wire.rs:42 and relay_endpoints() keep up to 3 endpoints per peer relay hint. is_host() accepts IP literals (wire.rs:283).
- targets() (transit.rs:129-161) keeps our relay, then one peer relay (the first that does not contain ours), then the peer's direct hints. It truncates to MAX_TARGETS=4, so at most 1 peer relay and 2 direct targets.
- TransitGuard::connect (transit.rs:338-356) walks every endpoint of the peer relay in order. For each it tries up to MAX_ADDRS_PER_HOST=4 resolved addresses one after another, until one accepts.
- The only filter on those addresses is peer_may_name (transit.rs:166-179). It blocks loopback, unspecified, multicast and broadcast. It does not check the phone's own interface addresses, so its comment "Never our own machine" is wrong.
- Callers (receive.rs:261, send.rs:266) add no further cap. The only limits are the 20 s handshake window around connect() and cancellation once the library has its connection elsewhere.
- So a peer can cause up to 12 relay attempts plus 2 direct attempts (14) to addresses it picks.

What stops me refuting it: SECURITY.md:59-63 reads as a bound on how many peer-chosen addresses the phone can be pointed at. The code allows about five times that many attempts. The one-by-one fallback also gives a remote peer a small reachability oracle into the phone's network. For example, with endpoints [lan:22, lan:80, attacker:4001], the attacker's relay only gets the relay line if the first two refused. Timing tells a refused connection apart from one that timed out.

Why the severity stays low and the scenario is overstated:
1. The loop returns on the first accept. So each target still opens at most one TCP connection, and the peer can never have more than three open. Read strictly, "open up to three outbound TCP connections" holds. Only the attempts (a SYN, then a refusal or a timeout) go past three.
2. The relay line and handshake bytes are fixed and go to exactly one address per target, not to every service in turn.
3. It needs the code and the user's consent for each transfer.
4. SECURITY.md already says the peer can make us "resolve relay host names it picks" and that "every wormhole client does the same". Upstream magic-wormhole 0.8.1 (transit.rs:1181-1215) tries 3 endpoints per relay hint for 2 peer hints, plus up to 50 direct hints. Sukkula is stricter than the library.
5. The own-interface point is only a wrong code comment. SECURITY.md lists only loopback, multicast and unspecified as excluded, and direct hints already allow the phone's own LAN IP. The Direct path makes the phone the relay itself, so only the library's fixed transit handshake goes out.

Verdict: a real but low-severity mismatch between the documented bound and the code. The fix is either to limit peer-named connection attempts (e.g. one endpoint or one resolved address for the peer relay), or to reword SECURITY.md to state the attempt count (up to 3 relay endpoints x 4 addresses, plus 2 direct). The peer_may_name comment should be corrected too.

kept.title: Server-requested hashcash (up to 20 bits, 256-byte resource) is minted synchronously on one of the engine's two tokio workers, beyond the reach of any timeout
kept.rule: S6 / SECURITY.md 'unbounded ... CPU use triggered by a mailbox server'
kept.description: check_welcome lets through a welcome that asks for hashcash of up to MAX_HASHCASH_BITS=20 over a resource of up to 256 bytes. The library mints it in RendezvousServer::connect (util.rs hashcash). That is a loop that never yields: each round formats a stamp of about 310 bytes, base64s the counter and SHA-1s it, about 2^20 rounds on average, and the number of rounds follows a geometric distribution. It runs inside a poll of the lib(t.handshake, ...) future, so tokio's timeout cannot stop it. The engine runtime has only two worker threads (hub.rs:227). One mint blocks half the runtime, and two concurrent wormhole operations against such a server block all of it, stalling LocalSend, Quick Share, consent timers and event delivery. The '20 bits ... well under a second' reasoning in the comment ignores the 256-byte resource and the tail.
kept.failure_scenario: A custom or malicious mailbox, or an on-path injector on the default ws:// mailbox that replaces the first welcome, sends {"type":"welcome","welcome":{"permission-required":{"none":{},"hashcash":{"bits":20,"resource":"<256 bytes>"}}}} on every connection. The user starts a wormhole send and a receive. Both workers spin in SHA-1 for seconds, sometimes several times the mean, and every other protocol's I/O and the consent timeouts stall until the mint ends.
kept.suggested_fix: Lower the cap (for example 16 bits and a 64-byte resource), or run the library's MailboxConnection::create/connect on a tokio::task::spawn_blocking thread or a dedicated runtime, so a mint cannot occupy an engine worker.

votes.reasoning:
The claim holds up, and I found nothing that refutes it. The impact is small, so it stays low.

What the code shows:
- **The guard lets it through.** `check_welcome` (`mailbox.rs:426-449`) passes a hashcash request when `bits <= 20` and the resource is at most 256 bytes.
- **The library mints it on the worker.** In magic-wormhole 0.8.1, `RendezvousServer::connect` (`rendezvous.rs`) matches `hashcash: Some(..)` first, before `none`, and calls `util::hashcash` directly inside the async fn. `util.rs` is a plain loop that never yields. Each round runs `format!` on the stamp, base64-encodes the counter and SHA-1s the result.
- **It is reachable.** The library only needs a `none` key present (W12), and `"none": null` works. The existing test `wormhole_hostile::a_modest_hashcash_is_minted_and_the_receive_goes_on` shows an 8-bit request going through the guard and being minted.
- **Nothing moves it off the worker.** `send.rs:89-95` and `receive.rs:99-102` run `MailboxConnection::create` / `connect` inside `lib(t.handshake, ...)`, which is `tokio::time::timeout` around `CatchUnwind`. There is no `spawn_blocking`, so the timeout cannot interrupt a mint. The runtime has 2 workers (`hub.rs:227`).
- **Two mints can run at once.** Sends are not limited by the connecting-receive slot, and up to 8 transfers can be active.

The comment's reasoning does not hold. It says 20 bits is "well under a second on the phone". I rebuilt the library's exact loop in a scratch crate (sha-1 0.10.1, base64 0.22.1) and timed 2^20 rounds on a 2.8 GHz Xeon without SHA-NI:
- a 1-byte resource: 0.58 µs per round, about 0.61 s in total;
- a 256-byte resource: 1.08 µs per round, about 1.13 s in total.

On aarch64, sha-1 0.10.1 uses software SHA-1 unless its `asm` feature is on, and magic-wormhole does not turn it on. Sailfish phones are ARM Cortex-A53/A55/A73-class chips, so the mean mint on the phone is probably several seconds. The number of rounds follows a geometric distribution: the chance of taking more than 3 times the mean is about e^-3, roughly 5%. That puts the tail around 10 s or more.

The project treats this kind of thing as a defect. SECURITY.md counts CPU use or hangs triggered by a mailbox server as in scope. The project already uses `spawn_blocking` for file opens and lists blocking runtime threads as defects in UPSTREAM-QUICKSHARE R10/R11. The 20-bit cap was meant to keep this under a second, and it does not.

Why the severity stays low:
- Each mint only happens when the user starts a wormhole operation, and it is bounded in expectation.
- Only a custom mailbox the user configured, or an attacker on the path to the plain `ws://` default, can cause it.
- One mint blocks only one of the two workers; stalling the whole runtime needs two wormhole operations at once.
- The effect is a delay of a few seconds, sometimes more, in LocalSend and Quick Share I/O and in consent timers. Nothing is corrupted, and no consent is bypassed.

kept.title: S7 not held on the Quick Share mDNS responder: any source is answered, legacy-unicast replies go to arbitrary addresses, and there is no per-IP rate limit
kept.rule: S7
kept.description: The reach policy is applied only to the phone's own interface addresses (IfPredicate on intf.ip()). mdns-sd's handle_query (service_daemon.rs:3440-3470) answers every querier that arrives on an enabled interface, whatever its source address. For a query whose source port is not 5353 it sends a legacy unicast response straight to the querier's IP and port (3613-3645, unicast_on_intf at 4933), which the kernel routes off-link if needed. Such replies are exempt from mdns-sd's only limit, one multicast per record per second. Sukkula applies no per-IP limit to Quick Share discovery replies at all: allow_discovery is used only on received announcements, keyed by the address they announce. S7 requires both halves: only private, link-local or ULA peers answered, and discovery replies rate-limited per IP. This is currently masked by the registration failure above and becomes live as soon as that is fixed.
kept.failure_scenario: With the service registered, a LAN host sends PTR queries for _FC9F5ED42C8A._tcp.local. with a spoofed source such as 8.8.8.8:4444 (or from 100.64/10, which Sukkula treats as non-private). Each query of about 50 bytes makes the phone unicast a PTR+SRV+TXT+A answer of about 300 bytes, with its device name and port, to that address, at whatever rate queries arrive. The result is an unthrottled reflector that answers non-private peers.
kept.suggested_fix: Patch mdns-sd's query path to drop queries whose source fails ReachPolicy or is not on the receiving interface's subnet. Refuse legacy-unicast replies to such sources. Rate-limit replies per querier IP, e.g. with Ctx::allow_discovery through the filter callback.

Everything the claim says about the code is correct. What it cannot do today is happen, because the service never registers, so this is a latent defect, not a live one.

- third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns.rs:44-47 is the responder's only S7 control. It is an IfPredicate on the phone's own interface address (`intf.ip().is_ipv4() && filter(intf.ip())`). Nothing in rqs_lib or sukkula-engine looks at the querier. Ctx::allow_discovery is called only in localsend/server.rs, localsend/discovery.rs and quickshare/discovery.rs:128, and the last one checks addresses that peers announce, not queriers.
- In mdns-sd, handle_read (service_daemon.rs:2668-2765) checks only that the receiving interface is known and that its IP version is enabled. It then passes pktinfo.addr_src to handle_query (3440) with no source-address check, no subnet check and no rate check. send_response (3613-3626) turns any query whose source port is not 5353 into a legacy-unicast reply to exactly that source IP and port. unicast_on_intf (4933) does a plain send_to, so the kernel routes the reply wherever the default route goes, off-link included. The per-record 1 s limit (apply_multicast_rate_limit) applies only to the multicast branch, so unicast replies bypass it.
- S7 in SPEC.md:119 ("only private, link-local or ULA answered; discovery replies rate-limited per IP") and SECURITY.md say both "a LAN protocol answering a peer outside private… ranges" is a vulnerability and "Quick Share … rate-limit discovery … per address". Once the responder is registered, it breaks both halves of S7. No test in the S7 row covers the mDNS responder: engine tests run with Options.mdns off, and rqs_lib has no MDnsServer test.

Why it is not live now: build_service passes `&name` (a base64url string with no ".local.") as the host name. ServiceDaemon::register calls check_hostname, which rejects any host name that does not end in ".local.". I confirmed this with a scratch build against mdns-sd 0.21.4 using the same arguments: `Err(Msg("Hostname must end with '.local.': IwECAwT8n14AAA"))`. run() then returns Err at `self.daemon.register(...)?`, and receive.rs logs that only at debug. With no registered service, handle_query answers nothing: PTR, the meta-query and the A/SRV lookups all iterate my_services, which is empty.

So the scenario as written ("With the service registered…") cannot happen at HEAD. The claim says so itself ("masked by the registration failure"). I did not refute it, because the underlying gap is real. The one-line fix that makes Quick Share discoverable (appending ".local." to the host name) makes the unfiltered responder live at once, and nothing else in the path stops it. At that point it answers non-private and spoofed sources, and it sends unthrottled replies of about 300 bytes (roughly 6x the query size) to arbitrary addresses. That would be medium. While it stays masked, the correct severity is low (latent). It should be fixed together with, or before, the registration bug.

The failure scenario begins "with the service registered", and the tree as it stands never gets that far. The claim itself says this ("currently masked by the registration failure above"). I checked that the masking is real.

**Registration always fails.**
- MDnsServer::build_service (third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns.rs:99-107) passes the bare gen_mdns_name() output as host_name. That output is 14 base64 characters with no ".local." suffix.

- ServiceDaemon::register calls check_hostname first (service_daemon.rs:539-541). check_hostname rejects any name that does not end in ".local." (4712-4715).

Today no Quick Share discovery reply goes to any address, spoofed or not, so S7 holds without being tested.

- handle_read (2668-2765) checks only that the packet arrived on an enabled interface. It never checks the source address.
- handle_query does not delay a PTR answer when the source port is not 5353. send_response then sets unicast_dest to that source address and skips apply_multicast_rate_limit.
- unicast_on_intf sends to that address through normal routing.
- Sukkula has no per-IP limit on this path; allow_discovery is used only on received announcements.

As a current defect, then, it is refuted: the scenario cannot happen in this tree. It is a latent trap. Whoever fixes the host name (for example `format!("{name}.local.")`) makes it live in the same change. The fix must also filter queries by ReachPolicy and subnet, refuse legacy-unicast replies to such sources, and rate-limit per querier IP. Once live, it would be a real S7 violation. I would rate it medium then: a small amplification (about 50 bytes in, about 300 out), plus the device name and port disclosed to a non-private address. It should be tracked with the registration-failure finding rather than on its own.

kept.title: S8 gate does not cover libdbus, which can start processes; only a runtime address check that no lint enforces
kept.rule: S8 / SECURITY.md S8 enforcement row
kept.description: libdbus can start a process in two ways. `autolaunch:` runs dbus-launch, and `unixexec:` forks and execs a program. The dbus crate's `blocking::Connection::new_session()` and `Channel::get_private(BusType::Session)` also fall back to autolaunch when DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS is unset. The only thing that keeps Sukkula off these paths is `check_address()`, which is called by hand at bus.rs:136 (and in a separate copy in quickshare/ble.rs). CI does not enforce this. clippy.toml (lines 10-13 and 126-127) bans only std/tokio `process::Command`. It bans none of `dbus::channel::Channel::open_private`, `Channel::get_private`, `dbus::blocking::{Connection,SyncConnection,LocalConnection}::new_session` or `ffidisp::Connection::get_private`. ci/check-deps.sh does not count libdbus as a process-starting part of the shipped graph. SECURITY.md says there is "one recorded exception: tokio's process module" and says the S8 row is enforced by clippy.toml and check-deps.sh. Neither of them would catch a libdbus process start.
kept.failure_scenario: Someone adds `dbus::blocking::Connection::new_session()` to the engine, or calls `Channel::open_private(env_address)` without going through `Bus::connect`. `cargo clippy -D warnings`, `ci/check-deps.sh` and every CI job still pass. On the phone, with DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS unset, or set to `autolaunch:` or `unixexec:path=...`, libdbus forks and execs a program inside the app. That breaks S8 while every listed gate stays green. The current code is safe only because both existing callers happen to call check_address first.
kept.suggested_fix: Add the dbus crate's autolaunching constructors and `Channel::open_private` to clippy.toml disallowed-methods. Lift the ban only on `Bus::connect` (and the quickshare BLE wrapper), the same way the file-API bans are lifted one function at a time. Record libdbus as an S8-relevant dependency in SECURITY.md and check-deps.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute the facts in the claim. It is an enforcement gap, not a live violation, so I am lowering the severity.

What I checked:

1. **clippy.toml has no dbus bans.** Its only S8 entries are `std::process::Command` (disallowed-methods ::new and disallowed-types) and `tokio::process::Command` (disallowed-types). It lists no dbus path. There is only one clippy.toml in the repo, and CI runs `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` against it. Nothing in ci/, .github/ or the Makefile greps for `open_private`, `get_private` or `new_session`.

2. **check-deps.sh does not treat libdbus as able to spawn processes.** Its SPAWN list is `async-process duct subprocess command-group process-wrap shared_child rusty-fork wait-timeout`. For dbus it checks only for a second D-Bus stack and the `vendored` feature (Q7). deny.toml handles dbus the same way.

3. **SECURITY.md reads as the claim says.** Line 134 names "one recorded exception: tokio's `process` module". The S8 row at line 176 names clippy.toml, check-deps.sh, the QML static checks and the rqs_lib patches. It does not name the `check_address` tests.

4. **The dbus 0.9.12 crate in the registry has safe constructors that can reach libdbus's process-starting transports:**
   - `Channel::open_private(&str)` calls `dbus_connection_open_private`.
   - `Channel::get_private(BusType)` calls `dbus_bus_get_private`.
   - `blocking::Connection::new_session()` and `new_system()` build on these.
   
   With `unixexec:`, libdbus forks and execs. If DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS is unset and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus is missing, libdbus falls back to its default session address, `autolaunch:`. `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` does not help here, because these APIs are safe.

For S3 the project bans every capable API down to rustix and lifts the ban one function at a time. S8 has no such ban for libdbus, and the table leaves out the tests that actually hold the rule.

Why I lowered the severity from medium to low:
- The shipped code does not violate S8. Both callers check the address first, and tests cover them.
- The failure needs someone to add a new unguarded dbus connection later, and it would still have to get through code review.
- Even after such a regression, the trigger is the process environment set by the launcher or Sailjail, never peer input. SECURITY.md's in-scope S8 item is spawning "because of anything a peer sent". On a Sailfish phone, DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS is normally set to a `unix:` socket, so the autolaunch fallback is unlikely in practice.

The finding is a real but low-severity hardening and documentation gap.

The claim holds as stated. Nothing in the codebase is violated today, so the severity is too high.

- clippy.toml bans only `std::process::Command`, `std::process::exit`, `std::process::abort` (lines 11-13) and the `std::process::Command` / `tokio::process::Command` types (lines 126-127). No `dbus::` path is listed anywhere.

- SECURITY.md line 134 does say "one recorded exception: tokio's process module". The S8 row (line 176) names clippy.toml, check-deps.sh, static_checks.py and the rqs patches. - Nothing elsewhere stops a new call site that skips `Bus::connect` or `quickshare::ble::advertise`. The two existing guards are hand-written copies: `bus.rs:309` `check_address`, and a second copy at `ble.rs:385`.

1. Nothing is violated today. `dbus` is used only by sukkula-engine (no other crate in Cargo.lock depends on it). Both `open_private` call sites run `check_address` first. The runtime refusal is tested end to end: `bus.rs` `only_unix_addresses_are_accepted`, `tests/bluetooth.rs` `missing_bluez_or_system_bus_is_unavailable` (which covers `unixexec:` and `autolaunch:`) and the `session_bus = unixexec:path=/bin/sh` case, and `tests/quickshare_ble.rs:452-453`. `session_address_from_env` also never falls back to libdbus's own lookup.
2. The failure needs two things. First, a future code change that bypasses `Bus::connect`. Second, a process environment that is hostile or incomplete, set by the launcher or sailjail, or by a local user. A peer cannot set it. SECURITY.md puts S8 in scope as "because of anything a peer sent", and a peer cannot reach this path. On Sailfish the session address comes from the user session or sailjail, so the autolaunch fallback would rarely be reached.

So this is a real gap in how S8 is enforced and documented, and a sensible hardening fix: ban the dbus constructors in clippy.toml, allow them one call site at a time, and name the address check in the S8 row. It is not an exploitable defect.

kept.title: A cancel during the Hello round trip still sends CreateSession, and the obexd session is orphaned
kept.rule: sessions left behind / cancel honoured (F-C5)
kept.description: `Bus::call` puts the message on the wire (`self.channel.send(msg)`, lines 153-156). It checks the cancel token only afterwards, in `wait_turn` (line 179/241). `obex::send` goes straight from `Bus::connect` to `create_session` (obex.rs:128-130), and `create_session` does not check the token first (obex.rs:156). Suppose the token is cancelled after the last `wait_turn` check of the Hello call and before CreateSession is sent, because the user cancels or the engine stops. Then CreateSession is written and the connection is closed microseconds later. The module docs (obex.rs:17-20) rely on obexd's owner watch to clean up an abandoned CreateSession. In obexd (client/session.c `obc_session_create` -> `obc_session_set_owner` -> gdbus `g_dbus_add_disconnect_watch`), that watch is added only when obexd handles the call. gdbus adds a disconnect-only watch without checking whether the name still has an owner (watch.c: `check_service` runs only when `connect != NULL`). dbus-daemon routes CreateSession and then handles our EOF in the same pass, so it sends NameOwnerChanged for our unique name before obexd's AddMatch exists. The watch never fires.
kept.failure_scenario: The user starts a Bluetooth send and taps Cancel at once, or the app is closed right after a send starts. The cancel lands during the Bus::connect Hello round trip. The adapter sends CreateSession(dest, opp), sees Cancelled, and drops the connection. obexd still pages the device and opens RFCOMM/OBEX, and registers /org/bluez/obex/client/sessionN owned by a unique name that no longer exists. RemoveSession requires sender == owner, so no one can remove it. The phone keeps an OBEX connection to the target device until obexd exits or the remote drops the link.
kept.suggested_fix: In `Bus::call`, check `cancel` before `channel.send`, or at least before CreateSession and before each SendFile in push_all/push_one.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute it. Each step of the claim holds when checked against the code.

- When the Hello reply is popped, the loop returns `Ok` without reading the token again.
- `obex::send` (obex.rs:128-130) goes straight from `Bus::connect` to `create_session`. `create_session` builds the call and sends it with no token check (obex.rs:153-157).
- So a cancel that lands after the last `wait_turn` of Hello, while `read_write` waits for the reply, still lets CreateSession be sent. The next `wait_turn` then returns Cancelled. `send` returns, and the Bus drop runs `dbus_connection_close`.
- Nothing in mod.rs (the `spawn_blocking` call site) guards this.

**Is CreateSession really written?** Yes. I checked the vendored libdbus in libdbus-sys-0.2.7. In dbus-connection.c, `_dbus_connection_send_preallocated_unlocked_no_update` runs `_dbus_connection_do_iteration_unlocked(..., DO_WRITING)` right away. `Channel::send` therefore puts the message on the socket; it is not only queued.

**Does the bus deliver it before it handles the disconnect?** Yes.
- libdbus queues the synthesized Disconnected only after all real messages ("all real messages have been queued up", dbus-connection.c:4236).
- In bus/dispatch.c the daemon routes the method call first. `bus_connection_disconnected` runs later, and it is what emits NameOwnerChanged.
- xdg-dbus-proxy (Sailjail) keeps this order: it flushes pending buffers before it closes the upstream side.

**Does obexd miss the disconnect?** Yes, on upstream BlueZ master, which I fetched.
- `create_session` (obexd/client/manager.c) passes `dbus_message_get_sender` to `obc_session_create`. That calls `obc_session_set_owner`, then `g_dbus_add_disconnect_watch`, then `g_dbus_add_service_watch`.
- In the service watch, the match is added with a blocking `dbus_bus_add_match` on `arg0=<unique name>`. `check_service` runs only `if (connect)`, so a disconnect-only watch never checks whether the owner still exists.
- By the time the AddMatch is in place, NameOwnerChanged has already gone out. `owner_disconnected` never fires.
- `remove_session` requires the sender to be the owner, so no one else can remove the session.

**Against the spec:** M-53 (F-C5) requires that no session is left behind. The obex.rs module docs (lines 17-20) promise that an abandoned CreateSession leaves nothing behind.

**Why the severity stays low:**
- The window is only about one Hello round trip plus building the message, normally well under a few ms, starting right after the blocking thread begins.
- A person tapping Cancel after the transfer appears in the UI will almost never land in it. It takes a slow session bus, or an engine stop at an unlucky moment.
- Even after the suggested fix, a cancel landing in the microseconds between the CreateSession send and the first `wait_turn` has the same race. The fix narrows the window; it does not remove it.
- The effect is an obexd session and a Bluetooth link left open, not data loss or a security issue.

kept.title: COMMAND_TIMEOUT can cancel set_receiving/set_settings mid-critical-section: final Receiving never emitted, statuses stuck at 'starting', adapter tasks detached
kept.rule: F-C1 / F-C5 (status shown correctly)

The future is then dropped: the JoinHandles are detached (their tasks keep running), the state lock is released, line 586 never runs, and HubState.statuses stays at Starting. The reply reports failure ('did not finish in time') although receiving was switched and some adapters did start.
kept.failure_scenario: BlueZ, or another daemon an adapter waits on, stops answering, so each Quick Share start or stop takes the full 15 s. The UI keeps showing 'starting' for every protocol until the next toggle, and the reply says the switch failed while listeners are in fact up.
kept.suggested_fix: Do not put the timeout around the part that holds the lock: bound lock acquisition separately. Or run set_receiving in a task that owns the guard and always emits the final Receiving. Or give up on commands still waiting for the lock and reply busy instead.

- set_receiving (547-587) does three things in order: it writes state.receiving and state.statuses (Starting), it emits Receiving (for on=true only), and it awaits each(). The final emit_receiving is at line 586.
- each() (667-707) runs every adapter in its own tokio::spawn task under ADAPTER_TIMEOUT = 15 s. If the command future is dropped, the JoinHandles are dropped and those tasks carry on detached.
- set_settings holds the lock through restart_receiving (591-600). That is one each() to stop and then one set_receiving, so up to about 30 s.
- ReplyGuard sends "the command did not finish in time".
- No other code emits Receiving or repairs state.statuses (grep shows only set_receiving and startup). So after a cancelled on=true command, HubState keeps Starting and the UI keeps 'starting' until the next switch.

The timing works. Take set_settings (0-30 s), then set_receiving (30-45 s), then a set_settings sent at t_C < 15 s. The third holds the lock from 45 to 75 s but has a deadline of t_C + 60. It is cancelled inside set_receiving after it set Starting, and in some orderings after the stop phase has already stopped the listeners.

The shell can queue commands like this:
- CoverPage's cover action calls setReceiving(!receiving) with no `switching` guard.
- SettingsPage sends set_settings every time the page is left.
- MainPage's toggle is guarded only against its own pending command.

kept.title: Async reply handlers pop or replace whatever page is on top, which can be another offer's consent dialog

kept.description: When a send command's reply arrives, sendTo()'s callback calls pageStack.replace(WormholeCodePage) (wormhole) or pageStack.pop() (other protocols) without checking that the Send page is still the current page. WormholeReceivePage.qml:41 does the same with pageStack.pop() when receive_wormhole is answered. Only `alive` is checked. 3. Emit offer 7. ConsentDialog is pushed (depth 3).

kept.title: A closed consent dialog can stay in the stack under the next one, showing a stale offer with a frozen countdown
kept.rule: F-C2 / F-C3
kept.description: When the engine closes an offer, or the countdown runs out, ConsentDialog.dismiss() calls answer(false). That emits finished(), and consentFinished() sets consentPage = null and restarts the 150 ms navigation timer while the dialog is still on the stack. The dialog removes itself through the 100 ms `closer` timer. If the stack is busy (for example, the dialog's own push animation) closer defers, and both timers poll pageStack.busy. When navigation's tick comes first after the transition ends, navigate() sees consentPage === null and pushes the next offer's dialog on top of the old one. closer then finds the old dialog Inactive, stops without rejecting (ConsentDialog.qml:290-297), and the old dialog is left in the stack for good.
kept.failure_scenario: A LAN attacker sends offer X, withdraws it about 100 ms after sending, and already has offer Y queued. X's dialog is dismissed during its push animation, navigation wins the race, and Y's dialog is pushed over X. After Y is answered, X's dialog comes back as the top page: sender, files, and "Declined automatically in 5x seconds" frozen, with working Accept and Decline buttons that do nothing (answered=true). The user believes they accepted X and nothing arrives. Any later offer's dialog is pushed on top of it again, because consentPage no longer tracks it.

I could not refute this one. The code does what the claim says, and I reproduced the race with the repo's own stubs and runner.

- In the dialog, `onOfferClosed` calls `dismiss()`. That calls `answer(false)`, which sets `answered` and emits `finished()` without sending anything, because `closedByEngine` is set. Only after that does it start the 100 ms `closer`.
- `finished()` runs `consentFinished()` (harbour-sukkula.qml:98-101). It sets `consentPage = null` and restarts the 150 ms `navigation` timer while X is still on the stack.
- Both timers poll `pageStack.busy`. If the dialog is dismissed during a transition, the first tick after the transition ends wins. With 100 ms and 150 ms periods, `navigation` fires first in part of that window, for example when the transition ends between 400 and 450 ms after dismissal.
- `navigate()` checks only `busy`, `consentPage === null` and `offers.count > 0`. Nothing stops it pushing Y on top of X.
- `closer` then finds the stack idle and X Inactive. It calls `stop()` without `reject()` (ConsentDialog.qml:97-110; the claim's 290-297 is the wrong line range). X stays in the stack for good.

- after the race: `mainPage / consentDialog:1(answered) / consentDialog:2`, with `consentPage=2`
- after accepting Y: `mainPage / consentDialog:1(answered)`, with `remaining` stuck at 60

- The buttons do not "do nothing". Silica's `accept()`/`reject()` still pop the stale dialog. The only effect of `answered=true` is that no answer reaches the engine.
- The countdown path is realistic only when the peer sets a very short expiry while the stack is busy. The main trigger is a withdrawal during the dialog's own push animation, or during any other transition.

No files are received without consent and no peer data is shown in a new way (S2 is unaffected). The harm is a confusing stale consent screen with a frozen countdown, in breach of the F-C2 and F-C3 UI promises. The user may think they accepted a withdrawn offer.
