- **Every command runs under the 60 s limit.** `Hub::spawn_command` (hub.rs:414-431) sends every command, including `ReceiveWormhole`, through `spawn_reply`. That wraps `hub.dispatch` in `tokio::time::timeout(COMMAND_TIMEOUT, ..)` with `COMMAND_TIMEOUT` = 60 s (hub.rs:85, 899). There is no exemption or separate path for wormhole receive.

- **The reply only comes after consent.** `Command::ReceiveWormhole` awaits `adapter.receive_code(code)` (hub.rs:521-524), which is `receive::start` (wormhole/mod.rs:278). `start` awaits `until_accepted` and only returns the `TransferId` after the user accepts. The module doc in receive.rs says the same: the UI gets its Reply when the offer is accepted.

- **The waits inside that one command add up to more than 60 s.**
  - `until_accepted` runs `mailbox::open` and `MailboxConnection::connect`, each bounded by `t.handshake` (`HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` = 20 s).
  - It then runs `Wormhole::connect`, also bounded at 20 s.
  - `read_offer` is bounded by `t.idle` (`NETWORK_IDLE_TIMEOUT` = 30 s).
  - Finally `ctx.offer` goes to `ConsentBroker::ask`, whose own `tokio::time::timeout(OFFER_TIMEOUT = 60 s)` only starts once the offer is shown.
  - So the command timer always starts before the consent timer, and both are 60 s. With any connection time above zero, the command timeout fires before the consent timeout. `COMMAND_TIMEOUT` is documented as "a last resort behind the adapters' own timeouts", but here it is hit in normal use.

- **What the user sees.** `offer_pending` hard-codes `expires_in: OFFER_TIMEOUT.as_secs()` (hub.rs:758). Engine.qml:534 sets `expiresAt` from it, and ConsentDialog.qml:275 counts down "Declined automatically in %n second(s)". The countdown is therefore too long by the connection time.

- **What happens when the command timeout fires.**
  - The whole `work` future is dropped, which drops the boxed `asking` future. `ConsentBroker::ask` documents that dropping it withdraws the offer, and the `Waiting` Drop at consent.rs:271 sends `Closed::Withdrawn`.
  - The session is dropped without `goodbye`, because `session.rs` has no Drop that sends one.
  - `spawn_reply` replies `Internal` "the command did not finish in time". WormholeReceivePage shows that as `errorText(internal)` = "Something went wrong." It should have been a refusal saying the offer was not answered in time.
  - The sender never gets "transfer rejected" and waits until its own timeout.

- **Nothing elsewhere prevents it.** The QML has no client-side timer that would step in, and no test checks this path.

It counts as a defect under the spec. F-C3 says unanswered offers are declined after 60 s. Here a wormhole offer is withdrawn before the 60 s the dialog shows, with the wrong error. If connecting and reading the offer take more than 60 s (the bounds allow up to 70 s), the command times out before the offer is shown at all.

The failure is in the safe direction: the offer ends sooner, and no data flows without consent. So this is not a security issue, and severity stays low.

kept.title: Any branch or dependency build script with packages:write can overwrite the SDK image that release builds pull by mutable tag
kept.rule: GitHub Actions supply chain: excessive token permissions / cache (image) poisoning
kept.description: The rpm job grants `packages: write` on every trigger, pull_request included (lines 77-82). At lines 104-108 it runs `docker login ghcr.io` with that token before running any PR-controlled script (scripts/build-rpm.sh, ci/build-sdk-image.sh) and before the cross-build step (line 188), which runs the build.rs of every crate in Cargo.lock. The only thing stopping a push from a PR is the workflow's own `if [ "$EVENT" != pull_request ]` (line 127), and a same-repo PR controls the workflow file and every script it runs. The image is pulled by mutable tag (`docker pull -q "$IMAGE"`, line 119). The tag is `sha256(ci/build-sdk-image.sh + BuildRequires)[:12]` (scripts/build-rpm.sh:54-55), so any branch that leaves those two inputs alone computes exactly main's tag. main, `v*` and dispatch builds then run that image `--privileged` with the checkout mounted (build-rpm.sh:155). They also lift /opt/cross out of it and compile the engine's C code with it. ci/build-sdk-image.sh:43-47 pins the upstream image by digest for exactly this reason, but the derived image is not pinned. sdk-image.yml (lines 297-303, 339-341) likewise gives packages:write to a workflow_dispatch that can run from any branch.
kept.failure_scenario: (a) A collaborator opens a same-repo PR touching scripts/build-rpm.sh. That puts it on rpm.yml's `paths` list, and nothing is merged. The PR adds `docker push` of a trojaned image tagged ghcr.io/<owner>/sukkula-sdk:5.2.0.15-aarch64-<main's hash>. The PR is then closed. The next `v*` tag build pulls that tag, compiles and links the engine with the trojaned /opt/cross GCC or mb2, and passes rpmvalidation. The release job then publishes the backdoored RPM with notes saying it passed the validator. (b) On any tag or dispatch run, a compromised crate's build.rs reads ~/.docker/config.json, left by the earlier login step, and pushes the same poisoned tag.
kept.suggested_fix: Do not grant packages:write to pull_request runs. Split image publishing into a job with `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` that runs no repo build code. Run `docker logout` before any build step. Pin the derived image by digest, recorded in the repo and checked after pull, instead of trusting the tag. Restrict sdk-image.yml to the default branch.

votes.reasoning:
Most of the cited code is quoted correctly. rpm.yml:82 grants packages: write to every trigger. Lines 104-108 run docker login before any repo script. Line 119 pulls the image by mutable tag, and line 127 is the only guard on the push. The tag is built at build-rpm.sh:54-55, and build-rpm.sh:155 runs the image --privileged. The sdk-image.yml citation is wrong: the file is 63 lines long, with packages: write at lines 20-23 and login and push at lines 47-61.

The claim still fails because neither scenario gives an attacker anything they don't already have. The permission it blames is not what makes either attack work.

(a) Same-repo PR. Only someone with write access can open a PR from a branch in this repo. Fork PRs get a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN no matter what `permissions:` says. The only PR bot, dependabot, covers github-actions and deliberately not Cargo (.github/dependabot.yml), and dependabot runs get read-only tokens anyway. A pull_request run also uses the workflow file from the PR itself, and the claim concedes this. So taking packages: write off PR runs in main's rpm.yml would not stop (a): the PR would add it back. The same writer can also push any branch with its own `on: push` workflow that asks for packages: write and pushes to ghcr. More directly, they can push a `v*` tag on a malicious commit. rpm.yml then builds that commit, and the release job (contents: write) publishes it with the "passed the validator" notes. The repo documents no tag rulesets, and it is a single-owner repo (muhnschein/sukkula). The poisoned-image route is a slower way to do what this actor can already do. No privilege boundary is crossed.

(b) Malicious build.rs. build.rs only runs if a malicious crate version is already in the reviewed, checksummed Cargo.lock on the tag or main. That code runs in the same job that compiles the release engine, so it can backdoor the shipped artifact directly. Poisoning the image would only add persistence. The suggested `docker logout` would not close this either: actions/checkout keeps the same packages:write GITHUB_TOKEN in .git/config by default.

What remains is a hardening gap, not an exploitable defect. The derived image is not pinned by digest, and the docs overstate things when they say a PR "cannot replace the one main builds with" (rpm.yml:94-97, BUILDING.md:182-185). That keying stops accidental collisions, not a writer acting in bad faith. docs/SECURITY.md's threat model is about hostile peers and says nothing about repo collaborators. If this is kept, it is low: pin the derived image by digest, defense-in-depth only.

I could not refute the mechanism. Everything it relies on is in the code, and nothing on the path stops it.

What holds:
- /home/user/sukkula/.github/workflows/rpm.yml:77-82 gives the job `packages: write` whatever the trigger. Same-repo pull_request runs keep that permission; fork PRs are cut to read-only.
- Lines 104-108 run `docker login ghcr.io` with that token. The credentials stay in ~/.docker/config.json for the rest of the job, and no step runs `docker logout`.
- Code from the PR or from third parties runs after the login: the cross-build at line 188, which runs every crate's build.rs, and scripts/build-rpm.sh.
- The image is pulled by mutable tag at line 119. The `SDK_IMAGE_ID` taken at line 132 is only used as a cache key and is never compared with a pinned value.
- The tag is `sha256(ci/build-sdk-image.sh + sorted BuildRequires)[:12]` (scripts/build-rpm.sh:54-55), so a branch that leaves those two inputs alone gets main's exact tag. GHCR tags can be overwritten.
- `v*` and dispatch builds then lift /opt/cross from that image and use it to compile and link the engine (lift/engine). They also run mb2 in it with `--privileged` and the checkout mounted (build-rpm.sh:155). The release job publishes whatever passed.
- The only thing stopping a push is the workflow's own `[ "$EVENT" != pull_request ]` at line 127. A same-repo PR controls that file.
- The derived image is not pinned by digest, although ci/build-sdk-image.sh:43-47 pins the upstream image by digest for exactly this reason.
- The project states the property this breaks. docs/BUILDING.md:182-185 says a PR "cannot replace the one main builds with; pull-request runs never push one", and rpm.yml:94-97 says the same. The claim shows that is enforced only by convention, not against hostile code.

Scenario (b) is the stronger one. .github/dependabot.yml says every Cargo change comes as a human-reviewed same-repo PR, not from Dependabot, whose PRs would get a read-only token. So a malicious build.rs in a proposed dependency runs in rpm.yml's PR run before review finishes. From there it can push main's tag with the stored credentials, and the poisoned image outlives the PR being rejected or the crate being removed.

What is wrong or overstated in the claim:
- The sdk-image.yml line numbers (297-303, 339-341) do not exist. The file is 63 lines; the permissions block is at lines 20-23 and the login at 47-51. The substance is correct: workflow_dispatch can run from any branch with packages:write.
- The suggested fix of dropping packages:write from PR runs does not close scenario (a). The PR controls rpm.yml's own `permissions:` block, and any write collaborator can get a packages:write GITHUB_TOKEN from a workflow on any branch. What actually fixes it is pinning the derived image's digest in the reviewed tree and checking it after the pull, plus running `docker logout` before any build step.
- Scenario (a) needs an insider with write access, whom GitHub's model largely trusts already. It adds a way around review and tag protection, not new access.
- In scenario (b), on tag runs the compromised crate is already compiled into the release. What the image adds there is persistence, and the path through an unmerged PR.

Severity: the impact would be severe, since the poisoned image would build and ship a backdoored release. But no outside attacker can do this: fork PRs get read-only tokens. It needs either a write collaborator or malicious crate code already running in a same-repo CI run. I rate it medium rather than high.

kept.title: Harbour source gate skips every '#' line, and rpm.yml never runs for src/ or crates/*.rs, so a hardcoded /home path passes every PR gate
kept.rule: Harbour gate hole (rpmvalidation 'Hardcoded path'; spec §7 Harbour gate on every PR)
kept.description: The 2.1 check (line 909) greps only `code_lines`, which drops every line whose first non-blank character is `#` (line 144). In C/C++ those are preprocessor lines like `#define`, and in Rust they are attributes such as `#[error("...")]`, which this codebase uses (crates/sukkula-core/src/offer.rs:169). Their strings end up in the shipped binary. The check also reads only *.rs/*.cpp/*.h/*.qml/*.js, so a string pulled in by `include_str!` from a .txt or .json file is never seen. The real validator runs `strings` over every file in the RPM and raises ERROR 'Hardcoded path' on `/home/(nemo|defaultuser)/`. rpm.yml's pull_request `paths` (lines 43-60) leave out crates/**/*.rs, src/** and qml/**, so for such a change nothing on the PR runs the real validator. The same filter also leaves out src/hardening.pri and src/dynamic.list, which decide main()'s export and stripping; for those, only the host stand-in link in the cpp job checks them.
kept.failure_scenario: A PR adds `#[error("cannot write to /home/defaultuser/Downloads/Sukkula")]` to an error enum in crates/, or `#define DL "/home/defaultuser/Downloads/"` used in src/bridge.cpp. ci.yml's harbour job passes (the line is dropped as a comment), rpm.yml is not triggered, and the PR merges. The next `v*` build's rpmvalidation.sh fails with ERROR 'Hardcoded path', or the package is rejected at Harbour intake if built another way.
kept.suggested_fix: In code_lines, drop only real comment syntax per language: `//`, `/* */` and ` * ` continuation lines, plus `#` only in files where it starts a comment. Do not drop `#define` or `#[...]`. Extend 2.1 to every file under crates/*/src and src/, or run `strings` over the host-built binary in the cpp job. Add crates/**, src/** and qml/** to rpm.yml's paths, or make the real validator run on every PR.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute the gap; I reproduced it. What limits it is that nothing non-compliant can ship without being caught.

What the code does:
- `code_lines()` (ci/harbour-check.sh:143-145) uses `grep -v -E '^[[:space:]]*(//|/\*|\*|#)'`. It is called only by check 2.1 (line 909), and only on *.rs, *.cpp, *.h, *.qml and *.js files. None of those languages uses `#` for comments, so the `#` rule never removes a comment. It removes only compiled lines: Rust attributes such as `#[error("...")]` (30 of them under crates/, e.g. offer.rs:169) and C/C++ preprocessor lines.
- docs/HARBOUR.md says 2.1 covers "anything compiled or shipped ... comments aside". Attributes and `#define` are neither comments nor excluded, so the check falls short of its own stated rule.

Reproduced on a copy of the tree in the scratchpad (repo files untouched):
- Unmodified: `harbour-check.sh` exits 0.
- With offer.rs:169 changed to `#[error("cannot write to /home/defaultuser/Downloads/Sukkula")]`: exit 0, and it prints "[2.1] no hardcoded /home/nemo or /home/defaultuser".
- With `#define DL "/home/defaultuser/Downloads/"` added to src/bridge.cpp: exit 0, same message.

Nothing else on a PR catches it:
- The `pull_request.paths` in rpm.yml (lines 43-60) leave out crates/**/*.rs, src/** and qml/**. The header comment and HARBOUR.md say this is on purpose, relying on the claim that "every Harbour question about them is answerable from the sources, and the harbour job asks them". This bug makes that claim false for `#` lines.
- ci.yml's cpp and cross jobs, tests/run-cpp-tests.sh and check-elf.sh run no `strings` or `/home` check.
- src/hardening.pri and src/dynamic.list exist and are included from the .pro, and are also outside rpm.yml's paths, as the claim says.

The real validator does reject it:
- I fetched upstream rpmvalidation.sh at the pinned commit. Its sha256 matches the value in ci/harbour/UPSTREAM.
- `validatesandboxing()` runs `strings` over every file in the package and calls `validation_error "Hardcoded path: $match"` on `/home/(nemo|defaultuser)/`.
- thiserror's Display impl and a `#define` literal that is used both end up as strings in the binary.

So the defect is real and breaks spec §7's promise that the source gate "asks every question ... a source tree can answer, on every pull request".

Why I lower severity from medium to low:
- rpm.yml runs the authoritative validator on every `v*` tag. It also runs on any PR that touches Cargo.lock, a Cargo.toml or third_party/, and those PRs are frequent.
- A violation therefore cannot reach a Harbour submission. The harm is late detection: a failed release build and a follow-up fix PR.
- The trigger is also uncommon: it needs a hardcoded home path inside an attribute or preprocessor line, and the app takes its directories from config at runtime.

The defect is real. I reproduced it on a scratchpad copy of the tree; no repository file was changed.

1. `code_lines` (ci/harbour-check.sh:143-145) runs `grep -v -E '^[[:space:]]*(//|/\*|\*|#)'`. Check 2.1 (lines 897-921) scans only `code_lines` of *.rs/*.cpp/*.h/*.qml/*.js. None of those languages uses `#` to start a comment, so the `#` in that pattern only ever drops real code: Rust attributes and C/C++ preprocessor lines. The selftest only covers the `///` doc-comment case (harbour-check-selftest.sh:319). Nothing there covers `#[...]` or `#define`, so dropping them is not a documented choice. docs/HARBOUR.md describes 2.1 as covering "C++, QML, the Rust crates and third_party/, comments aside".

2. Reproduction. The baseline copy passes ("[2.1] no hardcoded ...", exit 0). Two changes also pass with exit 0:
   - `#[error("the offer is empty")]` at crates/sukkula-core/src/offer.rs:169 changed to `#[error("cannot write to /home/defaultuser/Downloads/Sukkula")]`.
   - `#define SUKKULA_DL "/home/defaultuser/Downloads/"` added to src/bridge.cpp.
   As a positive control, `pub const X: &str = "/home/defaultuser/a";` does make it FAIL [2.1].

3. The real validator does reject this. I fetched rpmvalidation.sh at the pinned commit 7dd7dd5d; its sha256 91d0c833... matches ci/harbour/UPSTREAM. `validatesandboxing()` runs `strings` over every file in the package and calls `validation_error "Hardcoded path: $match"` on `/home/(nemo|defaultuser)/`.

4. rpm.yml's `pull_request.paths` (lines 43-60) leave out crates/**/*.rs, src/** and qml/**. docs/HARBOUR.md and rpm.yml's header say this is on purpose, because "every Harbour question about them is answerable from the sources, and the harbour job asks them". That makes the ci.yml harbour job the only per-PR guard for this rule, and it has this gap. No other CI step runs `strings` or greps a built binary for home paths: check-elf.sh and cross-build-rust.sh do not.

The secondary points hold but matter less:
- Files pulled in by `include_str!` (.txt/.json) are never scanned.
- src/hardening.pri and src/dynamic.list are also missing from rpm.yml's paths. The claim itself says the cpp job's host link covers them, and leaving src/ out of rpm.yml's paths is documented as intentional.

Severity: low rather than medium.
- rpm.yml runs the authoritative validator on every `v*` tag and on dispatch before any release, so a merged hardcoded path fails the release build before it can reach Harbour. The cost is late detection and a fix-up PR; no user impact or security impact.
- Whether a given `#[error]` string ends up in the binary depends on its Display impl being reachable. For example, `OfferError`'s Display appears unused in shipped code: its callers map it to fixed messages. `#define` literals that are used do end up in the binary.
- The trigger also needs someone to write a hardcoded home path, which the project already avoids.

It is still a real spec §7 gate hole, because the source gate fails to ask a question the sources can answer. The fix is small: drop `#` from the `code_lines` pattern.

kept.title: clippy.toml's S3 'one writer' ban misses tokio OpenOptions::default and Unix socket binds; rustix twins of banned process-state calls are unbanned
kept.rule: S3 (only sukkula-core writes files); SECURITY.md 'clippy.toml bans every call that creates, opens for writing...'
kept.description: The ban on opening for writing is expressed as `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new` (line 63). tokio 1.53.1 also has `impl Default for OpenOptions` (tokio-1.53.1/src/fs/open_options.rs:855), and that call resolves to `Default::default`, which is not on the list. Socket-file creation is banned only as `UnixListener::bind`/`UnixDatagram::bind` (lines 55-58). `std::os::unix::net::UnixListener::bind_addr` and `UnixDatagram::bind_addr` (stable since 1.70) and `tokio::net::UnixSocket::bind` (tokio-1.53.1/src/net/unix/socket.rs:153) are not banned; the engine enables tokio `net`. The file bans `std::env::set_current_dir` and `std::os::unix::fs::chroot` as process state shared with Qt, but the workspace enables rustix's `process` feature (Cargo.toml:35), and its `rustix::process::chdir`, `fchdir`, `chroot` and `umask` are not banned.
kept.failure_scenario: In crates/sukkula-engine, `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::default().write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(peer_derived_path)` compiles with no disallowed_methods error under `cargo clippy -D warnings`. That creates or truncates a file outside sukkula_core::inbox with no SafeName, O_EXCL or staging, and the 'one writer' guarantee the lint is meant to enforce is gone. Likewise, `tokio::net::UnixSocket::new_stream()?.bind(path)` creates a filesystem entry anywhere the sandbox allows.
kept.suggested_fix: Also ban the Default path (disallow the type `tokio::fs::OpenOptions` with per-site allows, or add a lint for `OpenOptions::default`). Add `std::os::unix::net::UnixListener::bind_addr`, `std::os::unix::net::UnixDatagram::bind_addr` and `tokio::net::UnixSocket::bind`. Add `rustix::process::{chdir,fchdir,chroot,umask}`, or drop the `process` feature where it is not needed.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this claim. I checked every part of it by building a small test crate in the scratchpad. It used a copy of the repo's clippy.toml, the same Cargo.lock pins (tokio 1.53.1, rustix 1.1.5) and the same tokio features as sukkula-engine. I ran `cargo clippy --offline` with clippy 0.1.97.

What clippy flagged, as expected:
- `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new()` (disallowed method)
- `std::os::unix::net::UnixListener::bind`
- `std::env::set_current_dir`

What compiled with no disallowed_methods error:
- `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::default().write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(p)`. `let o: tokio::fs::OpenOptions = Default::default()` also passed. tokio-1.53.1/src/fs/open_options.rs:855 has `impl Default for OpenOptions { fn default() -> Self { Self::new() } }`. The call resolves to the trait method, so the `::new` entry does not catch it.
- `std::os::unix::net::UnixListener::bind_addr` and `UnixDatagram::bind_addr`, used with `SocketAddr::from_pathname`.
- `tokio::net::UnixSocket::new_stream()?.bind(p)`. This is defined at tokio src/net/unix/socket.rs:153, and the engine enables tokio `net`.
- `rustix::process::chdir`, `chroot` and `umask`. `fchdir` exists in the same module. The workspace rustix dependency enables `process` (Cargo.toml:35), but only for `geteuid` in sukkula-core's dirfd.rs and store.rs.

No other check covers these paths. ci/harbour-check.sh 2.6 only matches lines that also name an installed /usr path. std::fs::OpenOptions has no Default impl, so std has no matching gap. The claim contradicts two statements in the repo:
- docs/SECURITY.md: "clippy.toml bans every call that creates, opens for writing, links ... std, tokio and rustix alike".
- clippy.toml's own comment: "Every call that can is listed".

So the lint gap is real, and it breaks the documented enforcement guarantee for S3 ("one writer").

Why I lower the severity to low:
- Nothing in the tree uses any of these paths today. My grep found no `OpenOptions::default`, `bind_addr`, `UnixSocket`, `chdir`, `chroot` or `umask` in crates/, so no file is actually written outside sukkula_core now.
- The failure scenario needs a future contributor to write the bypass and get it through review.
- The rustix process calls are about process state shared with Qt, not S3 file writes.

This is a defense-in-depth or tooling gap, not a vulnerability that can be exploited today.

Files: /home/user/sukkula/clippy.toml (lines 55-58, 63, 119-122), /home/user/sukkula/Cargo.toml:35, /home/user/sukkula/docs/SECURITY.md:97-104. The test crate is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-sukkula/666dedf2-0c07-5e29-a1c6-6a7efe87625a/scratchpad/lintprobe/src/lib.rs.

I could not refute the claim. Each part of it holds, and I tested it with the pinned toolchain.

**The code says what the claim says**
- tokio 1.53.1 is the version in Cargo.lock. Its src/fs/open_options.rs:855 has `impl Default for OpenOptions { fn default() -> Self { Self::new() } }`.
- The same tokio exports `tokio::net::UnixSocket`, whose `bind(&self, path)` is at src/net/unix/socket.rs:153. sukkula-engine enables tokio's `net` and `fs` features.
- The workspace's rustix 1.1.5 turns on `process` (Cargo.toml:35), and sukkula-core really uses it (`geteuid` in dirfd.rs and store.rs). So the feature cannot simply be dropped. That feature exports `rustix::process::{chdir, fchdir, chroot, umask}`.
- clippy.toml lists none of these: not `OpenOptions::default`, not `UnixListener::bind_addr` or `UnixDatagram::bind_addr`, not `tokio::net::UnixSocket::bind`, and not the rustix process calls. It does ban their counterparts `std::env::set_current_dir` and `std::os::unix::fs::chroot`.

**Test**
I built a throwaway crate in the scratchpad, not in the repo. It had a copy of clippy.toml and rust-toolchain.toml (clippy 0.1.97), the repo's Cargo.lock, and the same tokio and rustix features. I ran `cargo clippy --offline -- -D warnings`.
- A control call, `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new().write(true).create(true)`, was flagged.
- With the control removed, clippy finished clean on all of these:
  - `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::default().write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(p)`
  - `let o: tokio::fs::OpenOptions = Default::default()`
  - `UnixListener::bind_addr` and `UnixDatagram::bind_addr`
  - `tokio::net::UnixSocket::new_stream()?.bind(p)`
  - `rustix::process::chdir`, `chroot` and `umask`

The reason: a call to `OpenOptions::default()` resolves to `Default::default`, which is not `tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new`.

**No other guard closes the gap**
- ci/harbour-check.sh 2.6 greps for `OpenOptions` only on lines that also name an installed `/usr/share` or `/usr/bin` path, and it defers to "clippy.toml's S3 ban" as the broad rule.
- No other CI or test scans the Rust sources for these calls.
- docs/SECURITY.md says clippy.toml "bans every call that creates, opens for writing, links, renames, copies, removes or changes a file". Its enforcement table names these bans as the enforcement of S3.

So the documented, lint-enforced "one writer" guarantee has real holes.

**Why severity is low, not medium**
- Nothing in the current tree uses these calls. The only tokio OpenOptions uses in the engine are the two read-only `open_to_send` functions, which use `::new` with an explicit per-function allow.
- There is no runtime path from a peer to any of these calls. The failure needs a developer to write new code that uses one of them, so this is a gap in a defence-in-depth rule check, not a live vulnerability.
- `umask` can only remove permission bits, so it cannot widen sukkula-core's 0600 files.

kept.title: check-deps' S8 denylist lets URL/file-opening and spawning crates into the shipped graph
kept.rule: S8 (no process spawning, no URL or file opening); SECURITY.md 'ci/check-deps.sh bans process-spawning crates in the shipped graph'
kept.description: The only crate-level S8 enforcement is the name list `SPAWN='async-process duct subprocess command-group process-wrap shared_child rusty-fork wait-timeout'`. deny.toml's `[bans] deny` (lines 119-142) has no S8 entries at all. clippy.toml bans `std::process::Command` only in Sukkula's own crates, not in dependencies. The canonical S8-violating crates are missing: `open`, `opener` and `webbrowser` all run `xdg-open` or a browser through std::process::Command, and `nix`/`libc` wrappers expose fork/execve. None of them would trip check-deps or cargo-deny.
kept.failure_scenario: A dependency bump (the LocalSend core, magic-wormhole, mdns-sd, ...) starts depending on `open` to 'open the received file' or `webbrowser` for a link, and a received URL reaches it. `ci/check-deps.sh`, its selftest and `cargo deny check` all pass, and the phone build now contains code that spawns xdg-open on peer-influenced input, which S8 forbids.
kept.suggested_fix: Add open, opener, webbrowser, open-rs, xdg, nix (process/unistd features), pty-process, portable-pty, xshell, cmd_lib and execute to SPAWN, and mirror them in deny.toml `[bans] deny`. Better, make the check allow-list based: fail on any new crate in the shipped graph that has `std::process` in its source (grep the vendored sources in CI).

votes.reasoning:
The code matches the claim, so I could not refute it. The real impact is lower than claimed, though.

What the code says:
- In `ci/check-deps.sh`, line 66 sets `SPAWN='async-process duct subprocess command-group process-wrap shared_child rusty-fork wait-timeout'`. Lines 120-128 (lockfile) and 151-158 (shipped graph) only look for those names. The only other S8 check is tokio's `process` feature.
- The `[bans] deny` list in `deny.toml` covers only TLS, crypto, D-Bus and Apple/Windows crates. It has no S8 entry.
- `clippy.toml` bans `std::process::Command` and `tokio::process::Command`, but clippy only lints Sukkula's own crates, not dependencies.

Confirmed by running it. I added `open` and `webbrowser` to a scratch copy of Cargo.lock and put them in a saved shipped-graph tree. I then ran `ci/check-deps.sh --lock <scratch> --tree <scratch> --allow ci/deps-allow.conf`. It printed "check-deps: ok" and exited 0. No repository files were changed.

Why this counts as a gap under the docs:
- SECURITY.md's table says `ci/check-deps.sh` enforces "S8: no processes, no opening".
- SECURITY.md line 133 says it "bans process-spawning crates in the shipped graph".
- Every name in SPAWN is a process-runner or wait helper. None of them opens a URL or a file. So at the dependency level, the "no opening" half of S8 has no automated check.
- The script says its job is to stop "a dependency smuggling the thing into the tree". A future dependency change is exactly the case it exists for, so the scenario being hypothetical does not refute the claim.

Why low, not medium:
- There is no current violation. None of open, opener, webbrowser, nix, xdg, duct, subprocess or the others is in Cargo.lock today.
- Cargo updates are deliberately left out of `.github/dependabot.yml`. Every dependency change is a human-reviewed Cargo.lock diff with a reason for each crate (spec §6), and git dependencies are pinned by rev. That is a process safeguard, not an automated check.
- For harm, three things must all happen:
  1. An upstream protocol library starts opening URLs or files.
  2. Its input is influenced by a peer.
  3. Review misses the new crate.
  Step 1 would be an upstream vulnerability in its own right.
- A name denylist can never be complete anyway, since any crate can call `std::process::Command` directly. That is how the rqs_lib nmcli problem (Q6) arose. So adding these names is only a modest improvement to a best-effort net.

Parts of the claim that go too far:
- "The only crate-level S8 enforcement is the name list" leaves out the tokio `process` feature check.
- Suggesting `libc` wrappers be banned is not practical, because libc is everywhere.
- Adding open, opener and webbrowser to SPAWN, and mirroring them in `deny.toml`, is still a reasonable, cheap fix.

I couldn't refute this. The code matches the claim, and nothing else catches these crates. I found no current violation, though, so this is a gap in one layer of checking, not an exploitable hole.

What I checked:
- ci/check-deps.sh line 66 is `SPAWN='async-process duct subprocess command-group process-wrap shared_child rusty-fork wait-timeout'`. `open`, `opener` and `webbrowser` are not on it. The only other process check in the script is tokio's `process` feature.
- deny.toml `[bans] deny` names only crates for TLS, crypto, D-Bus and platform bindings. It bans nothing for S8.
- clippy.toml's bans on `std::process::Command` and `tokio::process::Command` apply only to Sukkula's own crates, not to dependencies.
- Test: I copied Cargo.lock to the scratchpad, added `[[package]]` entries for `open` and `webbrowser`, and ran `ci/check-deps.sh --lock-only --lock <copy>`. It printed "check-deps: ok" and exited 0. The shipped-graph step checks the same SPAWN list, so it would pass these crates too.
- None of these crates are in Cargo.lock today.

Why it still counts: S8 forbids URL and file opening. SECURITY.md says `ci/check-deps.sh` "bans process-spawning crates in the shipped graph" and lists it as S8 enforcement. `open`, `opener` and `webbrowser` spawn xdg-open or a browser through `std::process::Command`, and they are the usual crates for exactly what S8 forbids. The project's stated aim is to make "no processes" a CI-time fact rather than something reviewers must catch, and for these crates it is not.

Why I lowered the severity from medium to low:
1. It is hypothetical. It needs a deliberate dependency change, and those are controlled. The LocalSend core is pinned to a git rev and magic-wormhole to `=0.8.1`. rqs_lib is vendored and checked byte for byte by vendor-check.sh. Dependabot deliberately leaves Cargo out, and spec §6 requires a written reason for each new dependency. The new code would also have to open something built from peer data.
2. A list of crate names can never be complete. Any dependency can call `std::process::Command` directly, which is how upstream rqs_lib ran nmcli (see patch 0005). The patches and vendor review deal with that; check-deps was always a heuristic.
3. Part of the suggested fix goes too far. `libc` is in every graph, and `nix` is mostly used for things other than spawning, so neither can be banned. Adding `open`, `opener`, `webbrowser` and similar crates to SPAWN and to deny.toml is still cheap and reasonable.

kept.title: A 'v*' tag on any commit publishes a GitHub release; only the dispatch path is held to main
kept.rule: Release gate hole
kept.description: For workflow_dispatch releases the job refuses anything but refs/heads/main (lines 152-154). For a pushed `v*` tag it only checks that the tag's version equals the spec's Version (lines 149-151, 157-159). Nothing checks that the tagged commit is on main or passed ci.yml. The release job (line 235) then publishes with `--verify-tag`, and its notes say the package 'passed Jolla's Harbour validator ... Distributed through Harbour'.
kept.failure_scenario: Someone with push rights tags an unreviewed branch commit `v0.1.0`, and its spec says Version: 0.1.0. rpm.yml builds it, and the release job publishes 'Sukkula 0.1.0' from code that never went through review or ci.yml.
kept.suggested_fix: In the stamp step, for refs/tags/v*, require `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$GITHUB_SHA" origin/main` (fetch main first), and protect `v*` tags with a tag ruleset.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this; the code does what the claim says. In .github/workflows/rpm.yml, the stamp step (lines 148-156) only requires `GITHUB_REF == refs/heads/main` when `$RELEASE` (the dispatch input) is set. On a pushed `refs/tags/v*` it only checks that the tag's version matches the spec's `Version:` (lines 157-159). Nothing checks where the tagged commit sits: no merge-base/ancestor test against main, no check on ci.yml status, and `actions/checkout` fetches only the tagged commit. The release job's condition, `startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') || inputs.release != ''` (line 235), then publishes with `--verify-tag`, which only confirms that the tag exists. ci.yml runs only on push to main, on pull_request and on dispatch, never on tags, and the release job needs only `rpm`. There is no .github/rulesets or CODEOWNERS in the repo that would show v* tags are protected. The docs make "on main" a stated rule for both paths. docs/BUILDING.md says a release "is cut on `main`", and its steps say to "push the tag `v<version>` on the merge commit". So the workflow enforces that rule for dispatch but not for tags.

One point limits the impact, though it does not refute the claim. On a tag push, GitHub runs rpm.yml as it exists at the tagged commit, so someone with write access who wanted to get around a check could simply edit it out. For the same reason, the dispatch-path check also only catches mistakes; it is not a security boundary. Only a tag ruleset (a repo setting) actually stops a deliberate attempt. Still, the uneven mistake guard is real. If someone tags a PR branch commit before it is merged, or tags the wrong commit, a release goes out that looks official, whose notes say "Distributed through Harbour", and whose code skipped review and ci.yml. The rpm job's Harbour validator does still run on it. It takes someone with write access to the repo, and the result is a mis-cut release, not a compromise open to people outside the project. Severity stays low.

kept.title: Waiver scope differs between the two Harbour checks: the RPM validator ignores the check id, and an RPM-only waiver fails the source gate
kept.rule: Harbour gate: waivers
kept.description: `waived_line` reads `wid` but never compares it, and matches only subject and message globs (lines 176-179). harbour-check.sh matches only id and subject and ignores the message (lines 106-121), so a waiver written for it usually has message `*`, as its own selftest does (`1.8.3  openssl-libs  *`). Loaded by the RPM wrapper, such a line waives every validator ERROR or WARNING whose subject matches. Conversely, harbour-check fails any waiver that matches none of its own findings as stale (lines 965-975). A waiver meant for a validator-only finding such as 'file is not stripped!' therefore always turns ci.yml's harbour job red. The RPM waiver path that docs/HARBOUR.md and waivers.conf describe cannot be used, and its selftest exercises it only in a tree where harbour-check is never run (harbour-check-selftest.sh:441-460).
kept.failure_scenario: The team waives a source-check finding with subject /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula and message `*`. From then on, harbour-validate-rpm.sh also silently waives 'Binary must export main()', 'Cannot link to shared library', 'Hardcoded path' and 'file is not stripped' for the binary, and the RPM gate passes a package Harbour rejects.
kept.suggested_fix: Give each tool its own waiver namespace, for example an `rpm:` id prefix that harbour-check skips in its stale test and the RPM wrapper requires. Make harbour-validate-rpm.sh reject `*` as a message glob.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this. Both halves of the claim hold up, and I reproduced each in a scratch copy of the tree (git archive into the scratchpad; the repo itself was not touched).

**What the code does**
- **RPM wrapper (`ci/harbour-validate-rpm.sh:171-182`):** `waived_line` reads `wid` and only checks that it is non-empty. It then matches the subject glob and the message glob. The validator's `KIND|subject|message` lines carry no check id, so the wrapper has nothing to compare `wid` against, and every waiver line in `waivers.conf` is live for the RPM gate whatever id it names.
- **Source check (`ci/harbour-check.sh`):** `waived()` at lines 106-121 matches only the id and the subject and ignores the message field. The stale test at lines 965-975 fails any `"$wid $wsubject"` key that none of harbour-check's own findings used.

**Reproduced: an RPM-only waiver breaks the source gate**
- I appended `1.2.4 /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula *file is not stripped* # rpm-only` to the copy's `waivers.conf`.
- `harbour-validate-rpm.sh --log`, fed `WARNING|/usr/bin/harbour-sukkula|file is not stripped!`, exits 0 with the finding WAIVED.
- `harbour-check.sh` then exits 1 with `stale waiver '1.2.4 /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula' ... matches nothing`. The baseline tree exits 0.
- So an RPM-only waiver, which the `validate-rpm` header (lines 14-15), `waivers.conf` and `docs/HARBOUR.md` all describe, turns ci.yml's `harbour` job red. Giving the line an id and subject that match a live source finding is not a general workaround.
- The selftest (`harbour-check-selftest.sh:438-460`) exercises the RPM waiver only in a tree where harbour-check is never run, so it misses this.

**Reproduced: a `*` message glob waives everything about a path**
- The docs promise that a waiver "never excuses every finding about a path". I added `1.2.3 /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula * # source waiver`, the same shape as the selftest's `1.8.3 openssl-libs *`.
- The RPM wrapper then WAIVED `Cannot link to shared library`, `Binary must export main()` and `file is not stripped!` together and exited 0, despite a FAIL verdict.

**Caveats that limit severity but do not refute**
1. The exact scenario is contrived. The only source finding with subject `/usr/bin/harbour-sukkula` is 1.2.3 (line 338), which fires only when that path is missing from `%files`, and then the RPM would not normally contain it. The same over-waiving does apply realistically to 1.2.1, 1.2.4 and 1.2.6 path subjects, which the validator also reports on.
2. The over-waiving only happens if an author writes `*` as the message. Writing a real message glob avoids it, though harbour-check gives no feedback on the message field and its selftest models `*`.
3. `waivers.conf` is empty. SPEC §2 and HARBOUR.md say it is meant to stay empty, and adding a waiver is a deliberate, reviewed change. So this is a latent inconsistency in the gate's design, not a live bypass: one direction fails closed, and the other needs an explicit broad glob.

Low severity is appropriate.

kept.title: Concurrency groups keyed on the bare head_ref let unrelated fork PRs cancel each other's CI
kept.rule: CI availability
kept.description: `group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.ref }}` with cancel-in-progress. For fork PRs `github.head_ref` is only the branch name, with no owner or PR number. rpm.yml:65 uses the same key. PRs from different forks with the same branch name, very often `main` or `patch-1`, share a group.
kept.failure_scenario: Contributor A's fork PR from `main` is mid-run. Anyone opens or pushes to another fork PR whose branch is also `main`, and A's ci run is cancelled. Repeated pushes keep A's required checks from ever completing. This cannot turn a check green, but it blocks merges.
kept.suggested_fix: Key on the PR number: `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}`.

votes.reasoning:
The claim holds. .github/workflows/ci.yml:19-21 has `group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. On a pull_request event, `github.head_ref` is just the head branch name. It does not include the fork owner or the PR number. Fork PR runs execute in the base repository, and concurrency groups are scoped per repository. So two open PRs from different forks whose branches share a name (`main`, `patch-1`) both land in `ci-pull_request-main`. The newer run cancels the older one's in-flight run.

Nothing else prevents this:
- No other part of the workflow separates these runs; the comment above the key only covers the push case (why `github.ref` rather than `run_id`).
- No spec text limits contributions to in-repo branches. SPEC §7 and SECURITY.md say nothing about concurrency or forks.
- SPEC §7 makes every ci.yml job a merge gate, so a cancelled required check blocks the merge.

The same collision also happens between an in-repo PR branch and a fork branch with the same name. It also happens between two PRs from one branch into different bases.

rpm.yml:64-66 is not literally 'the same key'. It is `rpm-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.run_id }}`, with a run_id fallback instead of ref. For pull_request events, though, it is keyed on the bare head_ref too, so it collides the same way. That wording slip does not weaken the finding.

The impact is overstated:
- The 'anyone can keep A's checks from ever completing' angle is weakened: by default, workflows on a first-time contributor's fork PR wait for maintainer approval.
- A cancelled run can be re-run.
- It never turns a check green.

The accidental case, contributors sharing common branch names like `main` or `patch-1`, is realistic, and wasted runs plus blocked merges are a real availability nuisance. It is a real defect with low severity. The suggested fix is the right shape: key on `github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref`, or keep event_name in the key.

kept.title: check-elf.sh does not check the 'only main exported' rule SECURITY.md credits it with, so the shipped binary's exports are never checked
kept.rule: Test does not test what it claims
kept.description: docs/SECURITY.md:182 lists `ci/check-elf.sh (stripped, only main exported, ...)` as enforcing the linking guarantee. check-elf.sh only requires that `main` is a defined FUNC in .dynsym (lines 116-123) and accepts any number of other exports. The 'only main' rule is enforced only by tests/run-cpp-tests.sh, on a host link built with the stand-in tests/cpp/sailfishapp/features/sailfishapp.prf. The real SDK link of /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula, run by build-rpm.sh check(), does not check it.
kept.failure_scenario: The SDK's real sailfishapp.prf or ld differs from the stand-in, for example in how -rdynamic interacts with --dynamic-list and --exclude-libs. The packaged binary then exports Bridge methods and the sukkula_* entry points. build-rpm.sh check and rpm.yml pass, even though the documented enforcement says this cannot happen.
kept.suggested_fix: Add an `--only-main` option to check-elf.sh that runs the cpp job's dynsym filter, pass it from scripts/build-rpm.sh check(), and add a case to check-elf-selftest.sh.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute this claim. The code says what the claim says.

- **What check-elf.sh checks:** lines 116-123 of `/home/user/sukkula/ci/check-elf.sh` run an awk filter for a defined GLOBAL FUNC named `main` in .dynsym, then `grep -q .`. So the check passes as long as `main` is present, no matter what else is exported. None of its options (`--glibc-ceiling`, `--libc-start-main`, `--main-export`, `--stripped`, `--readelf`) limits the other exports. Git history shows it never did: the script had no such check at fc87d9b, the commit that added the SECURITY.md row.
- **What the docs say:** `docs/SECURITY.md:182` names `ci/check-elf.sh` as enforcing "stripped, only `main` exported, RELRO/BIND_NOW/PIE, allowed libraries only". The same file says "When a row changes, change the code or test it names". So the enforcement table is wrong on this point. `docs/HARBOUR.md:121-124` and the rpm.yml comment describe check-elf accurately ("`main()` a defined dynamic symbol"), so the only wrong entry is the SECURITY.md row.
- **Nothing else checks the shipped binary:** `scripts/build-rpm.sh check()` (lines 182-183) calls check-elf with `--main-export --stripped --libc-start-main 2.34 [--glibc-ceiling]`, then runs Jolla's validator (`ci/harbour-validate-rpm.sh`). As far as I know, and that validator is not vendored in the repo, it requires `main` to be exported but does not limit other exports. rpm.yml only runs `build-rpm.sh check`.
- **Where the rule is enforced:** only in `tests/run-cpp-tests.sh` `elf_checks` (lines 72-82, used at line 199). That runs on a host x86 link built with the stand-in `tests/cpp/sailfishapp/features/sailfishapp.prf`, not on the SDK-built aarch64 `/usr/bin/harbour-sukkula`.
- **Selftest:** `ci/check-elf-selftest.sh` has no case for extra exports. Its "good" binary would still pass with an added default-visibility function.

**How likely a real leak is:** probably unlikely today. The stand-in prf copies the real SDK feature's flags (`-fvisibility=hidden`, `-pie -rdynamic`). `src/hardening.pri` adds `--dynamic-list` and `--exclude-libs,ALL`, which work the same way in any GNU ld. So the failure scenario is speculative. Still, the defect is real: the gap between what is documented and what is enforced is exactly the "test does not test what it claims" category.

**Severity:** low, as claimed. It is a missing CI check and an overstated enforcement table, not an exploitable problem. Extra exports from an executable are about Harbour tidiness and hardening, not memory safety or data exposure.

kept.title: fuzz-smoke passes no -max_len, so the 64 KiB assertions in text_message, command_json and start_config can never fail in CI, contrary to fuzz/README.md
kept.rule: S6 (64 KiB per text or JSON message); gate with a hole
kept.failure_scenario:
Two example regressions that pass fuzz-smoke on every pull request:
- `text::message` cuts at MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES inside a grapheme, leaving a trailing space or a combining mark without a base.
- `parse_command` starts accepting a 65 537-byte command.

In both cases no input the fuzzer generates is long enough to reach the branch.
kept.suggested_fix: Pass `-max_len` per target from one table: 70000 for text_message, command_json, start_config and localsend_prepare_upload, 4096 otherwise. Commit one seed just over the cap for each of those targets.

votes.reasoning:
The facts in the claim are correct. The claim overstates the impact.

**The gap is real.**
- scripts/fuzz-smoke.sh:64 builds `args` from only these four flags: `-max_total_time`, `-rss_limit_mb=2048`, `-timeout=10` and `-print_final_stats=1`. Nothing else in the repo passes `-max_len`. The only mentions are fuzz/README.md:103 and :109.
- The vendored libFuzzer (libfuzzer-sys-0.4.13, FuzzerLoop.cpp:797-807) sets `kMinDefaultLen = 4096`. When MaxLen == 0 it calls `SetMaxInputLen(std::clamp(MaxSize, kMinDefaultLen, kMaxSaneLen))`, so the limit is the larger of 4096 and the biggest corpus file.
- The committed seeds are small: text_message 62 B, command_json 149 B, start_config 120 B at most.
- fuzz/corpus/ is gitignored, and the CI job does not cache it. rust-cache covers only the fuzz workspace's target and cargo directories. So every CI run fuzzes with max_len = 4096.
- text_message uses `from_utf8_lossy`, which can at most roughly triple the input, to about 12 KiB. `text::message` (text.rs:202-261) only drops characters or passes them through; it never grows the text. The output therefore cannot pass MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES (65536), and neither the cap branch nor the oracle's size check (tests/common/oracle.rs:144) is reached.
- command_json and start_config reject invalid UTF-8, so they see at most 4096 bytes. Their `json.len() > MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES` branch, and `assert_ne!(e, TooLarge)` at exactly 65536 bytes, cannot run.
- fuzz/README.md:109-110 says text_message takes `-max_len=70000` "so that the 64 KiB cap is reachable". The CI gate does not do this.

**Why medium is too high.**
- The line saying 70000 is in the manual "Running" section. The README's CI section describes the smoke flags accurately and does not claim `-max_len`, so the mismatch is looser than "contrary to fuzz/README.md" suggests.
- More importantly, the `test` job checks the same 64 KiB rules deterministically on every push:
  - properties.rs:238 `huge_messages_are_capped` repeats a nasty unit 8,000-20,000 times and checks both `out.len() <= MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES` and the full `message_violation` oracle: trimmed, no mark without a base, and so on.
  - text.rs:338-340 and :473-477 are exact edge tests at MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES - 1 for the space case and the combining-mark case.
  - api.rs:652-659 asserts that a command over 64 KiB is refused as `TooLarge`.
- So the first example regression, cutting inside a grapheme and leaving a trailing space or a bare mark, would very likely be caught outside fuzz-smoke.
- What stays uncovered is small, such as an off-by-a-few-bytes loosening of `parse_command` or `parse_start_config` at the boundary. That would still be bounded, because the FFI reader in sukkula-ffi/src/lib.rs:258 caps reads separately.

**Verdict.** This is a real gap between the documentation and the CI gate, and it weakens defence in depth, but the main rule has other checks. Low severity, not medium.

The facts in the claim are correct. The failure scenarios are overstated, because other CI tests already catch both example regressions.

Confirmed:
- scripts/fuzz-smoke.sh:64 builds its args from -max_total_time, -rss_limit_mb, -timeout, -print_final_stats and an optional -dict. It never passes -max_len.
- cargo-fuzz 0.13.2 adds no -max_len of its own. Its source only mentions -max_len in help text.
- libFuzzer (libfuzzer-sys 0.4.13, FuzzerLoop.cpp:796-807) sets MaxLen to std::clamp(largest corpus file, 4096, 1<<20) when none is given.
- In CI, fuzz/corpus/ is empty: .gitignore:28 excludes it, and rust-cache only caches the target directory. The committed seeds are small: text_message at most 62 B, command_json at most 149 B, start_config at most 120 B. So the effective max_len is 4096.
- text_message runs from_utf8_lossy on at most 4096 bytes, which yields at most about 12 KiB. text::message never grows its input. So the cap at text.rs:245/253 and oracle.rs:144 is never reached during fuzzing.
- The same holds for command_json.rs:51/67-68 and start_config.rs:115/137: the json.len() > MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES branch cannot run. Those assertions can never fail in CI.
- fuzz/README.md:109-110 says "text_message takes -max_len=70000, so that the 64 KiB cap is reachable". The CI smoke does not follow that.
- SECURITY.md:181 counts these targets as CI checks that assert the S-rules. So the gate has the hole the claim describes, and that contradicts the docs.

Why this is only low severity:
- CI does not rely on the fuzz smoke for the 64 KiB cap.
- For text::message, text.rs tests 473-477 cover exactly the trailing-space and combining-mark edge cases at MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES-1. text.rs:338 covers truncation on a character boundary. properties.rs huge_messages_are_capped repeats strings to 8k-20k units and checks both out.len() <= MAX and oracle::message_violation.
- For parse_command, api.rs:653-659 asserts TooLarge on an input over 64 KiB. ffi.rs:145 asserts SUKKULA_ERR_TOO_LONG for MAX+1 bytes.
- So both regressions in the failure scenario would pass fuzz-smoke but fail other CI jobs. They would not merge.

The defect is real but limited: dead fuzz assertions in CI and a mismatch between the smoke script and the README and SECURITY.md. It is not an S6 regression that CI would let through.

kept.title: No kill-during-write (chaos) test, and what a kill leaves behind is not cleaned up: store temporaries, a final-named partial from the copy fallback, a split key/cert pair
kept.rule: S3; SECURITY.md:105-111 ('Any failure, cancel or panic deletes it')
kept.description:
clove's /home/user/muhnschein/clove/ci/chaos.sh does three things: it SIGKILLs the real daemon during state writes and checks each kill landed; it plants torn `.tmp` files and requires a restart to ignore them; and it makes the state directory unwritable under a running daemon.

Sukkula has no kill test; the only kills in its tests target the D-Bus fixtures. What a kill leaves behind is not handled:

- The EXDEV/EPERM copy fallback (inbox.rs:457-477) creates the final-named file first and relies on the `Placing` drop guard to remove it. A drop guard does not run on SIGKILL.
- The key and the certificate are written as two separate renames (identity.rs:107-114).

- During a settings save: a `.settings.json.<hex>.tmp` stays in `~/.local/share/sukkula/sukkula` for good, one per kill.
- During the copy fallback, when ~/Downloads is on a filesystem without hard links: a truncated `photo.jpg` stays in ~/Downloads/Sukkula under its real name. It looks exactly like a complete file, contrary to 'Any failure, cancel or panic deletes it'.
- Between the key and certificate renames on first run: the next start replaces the identity, and peers see a new device.
kept.suggested_fix: Sweep `.*.tmp` in `Store::open`. In the copy fallback, copy into a `.part` name in the target directory and link or rename it into place, so a kill never leaves a final-named partial. Write the key and certificate as one file, or with one rename. Add a chaos script that SIGKILLs the real engine during set_settings, identity creation and a receive, and checks what is left on disk.

1. Store temporaries (store.rs:122, the cited line): real. `Store::write` creates `.{name}.{hex}.tmp` and deletes it only when `replace` returns an error (store.rs:124-126). Neither `Store::open` (store.rs:75-81) nor anything else in the engine removes leftover `.tmp` files; the only sweep is `inbox::sweep_stale`, and it covers only `*.part` in `.partial`. So a SIGKILL between the `openat` and the `renameat` in `replace()` leaves an orphan for good. The harm is small:
   - the orphan holds a few hundred bytes and sits in the private 0700 data directory;
   - `check_name` rejects a leading dot, so the orphan is never read;
   - the store's own promise ("a crash leaves the old version") still holds.

2. kept.title: Wormhole receive consent is killed by the 60 s command timeout, before the offer's own 60 s runs out
kept.rule: F-C3, F-MW2
kept.description: Every command runs under `COMMAND_TIMEOUT` = 60 s (hub.rs:85, 899). `receive_wormhole` returns only after the user has answered. So the command deadline always fires before the consent deadline. When it fires, the future is dropped, the offer is withdrawn (`Closed::Withdrawn`), and the reply is `internal: the command did not finish in time`. The UI countdown (Engine.qml:534) still shows 60 s.
kept.failure_scenario: `wormhole send file`, then type the code on the phone. The mailbox and PAKE take 3 s and the dialog shows 'Declined automatically in 60 seconds'. At about 57 s the dialog disappears while it still shows 3 s left. An Accept pressed in that window returns not_found, and WormholeReceivePage shows 'Something went wrong.' The sender gets no 'transfer rejected'. With a slow mailbox (connect plus PAKE plus the offer taking 60 s or more), the command dies before consent is ever shown. No test waits before answering (tests/wormhole.rs:831-850 answers at once).
kept.suggested_fix: Return the reply for receive_wormhole as soon as the code is accepted by the mailbox, and report acceptance through events. Or exempt this command from COMMAND_TIMEOUT and bound it by its own phases (handshake + idle + OFFER_TIMEOUT). Add a test that answers after 58 s under a paused or short clock.

That covers the mailbox connect (`t.handshake`, 20 s), the PAKE (20 s), `read_offer` (`t.idle`, 30 s) and `ctx.offer(raw)` (receive.rs:44-57, 90-150). The receive.rs module doc says the same: the command stays pending until the offer is accepted, and the user's wait is bounded by "the consent timeout".

Engine.qml:534 turns that into a 60 s countdown. Because the dialog's 60 s starts after the handshake, the command deadline always fires first, by however long the connect, PAKE and offer took.
- When the command times out, the future is dropped. The `Waiting` guard's Drop (consent.rs:270-279) removes the entry and emits `Closed::Withdrawn`. Session has no Drop impl, and `goodbye` only runs on the explicit paths, so the sender gets no "transfer rejected". 2. **The consent clock starts later, so the command deadline always fires first.** The engine's broker is `ConsentBroker::new` (hub.rs:217), which uses `OFFER_TIMEOUT` = 60 s. `ConsentBroker::ask` (consent.rs) emits `Pending` and only then starts `tokio::time::timeout(self.inner.timeout, &mut rx)`. That clock starts at T0 + (connect + PAKE + read offer), while the command clock started at T0. If the user never answers, the command deadline is always hit first. The `Refusal::TimedOut` branch for wormhole receive ("the offer was not answered in time", then `goodbye(Some(REJECTED))`) can therefore never run.

3. **What happens when it fires.** The dropped future drops `asking`, and `Waiting::drop` (consent.rs) emits `Closed::Withdrawn`. Meanwhile the UI countdown is built from `expires_in: OFFER_TIMEOUT.as_secs()` (hub.rs:758, Engine.qml:534), so it still shows the few seconds that connecting used.

5. **It breaks the spec.** F-C3 says "declined after 60 s", and MANUAL-TESTS M-11 says "the sender sees a refusal". kept.title: F-C1: Magic Wormhole cannot be disabled in Settings, and the per-protocol disable is untested at engine level

- `tst_send.qml:223` pins the current behaviour ("wormhole has no switch"), but SPEC.md, FFI.md and the §8 decisions give no reason for leaving it out.
- SPEC F-C1 says "each protocol can be disabled in Settings", and §1 lists Wormhole as one of the four protocols.
- One could argue F-C1 only means receivers, and Wormhole is `send_only` with no listener. That argument fails because the implementation gives send-only Bluetooth a switch (`bluetooth.enabled`, "Offer Bluetooth as a send target"), so its own reading of "each protocol" covers non-receivers. Leaving Wormhole out is an undocumented departure from the spec.

2) The engine-level test gap is real.
- `enabled()` is honoured in four places: `set_receiving` (`hub.rs:561`), `statuses` (650), `StartDiscovery` (471) and `adapter()` (628, which gives Unavailable for send and the other commands).
- No Rust test anywhere sets `localsend.enabled`, `quickshare.enabled` or `bluetooth.enabled` to false.
