That is reached only through `Command::StartDiscovery` (hub.rs:467). The QML sends that command in exactly one place: `SendPage.qml:169`, when the Send page becomes active. Neither `set_receiving` nor `start_receiving` starts discovery or the nudge.
   - The code's own docs agree. ble.rs:1-5 says the nudge runs "while Sukkula looks for Quick Share devices to send to" and makes "Android phones nearby with Quick Share on start announcing their mDNS service". quickshare/mod.rs:30-33 says the same.
   - SPEC F-QS2 and HARBOUR.md:142 describe it the same way: it makes Android phones reveal *their* service.
   - The automated test (`tests/quickshare_ble.rs`, `discovery_runs_the_nudge_and_stops_it_in_time`) also drives it through `start_discovery`.

2. **M-31 tests the receiving direction and cannot fail because of the nudge.** It turns Receive on and opens the Android phone's share sheet, so the Android phone is the sender. With visibility set to Everyone, the Jolla's receiver already announces itself over mDNS (mod.rs:9-11). The nudge never runs in this test. The pass condition "or appears after a moment over mDNS" is met by mDNS alone, so a broken nudge still passes. The note "(the BLE nudge worked)" gives the wrong cause.

3. **The Settings text describes the nudge backwards.** SettingsPage.qml:261 says "Announce over Bluetooth that this phone is receiving, so Android phones look for it." What the nudge actually broadcasts is the Quick Share beacon that says "a device nearby is sharing", while the Jolla is sending. It makes Android phones announce themselves; it does not make them look for the Jolla. The wrong text is also in the sv, de and fi translations. The translator comment at line 258 has the same mistake.

**Limits on severity.** SPEC §7 only asks for "at least one automated test or a named manual test". F-QS2 has an automated test against a fake BlueZ, so the coverage rule itself is formally met. F-QS2 is also best effort by design. What remains is a hardware test that names F-QS2 but cannot catch a broken nudge, plus user-facing text that describes the nudge backwards. That is a documentation and test-design defect with no runtime or security impact, so low is right.

kept.title: §7 reference-client loopback layer: wormhole interop never runs in CI, and there is no rquickshare interop
kept.rule: §7 Adapters layer
kept.description: §7 requires loopback transfers against the reference clients (LocalSend CLI, wormhole CLI, rquickshare) as `cargo test`. All four wormhole_interop tests are `#[ignore]` and need SUKKULA_PY_WORMHOLE, which no CI job or Makefile target sets (a grep of .github/, ci/, scripts/ and the Makefile finds neither `--ignored` nor SUKKULA_PY_WORMHOLE). Quick Share has no reference-client test: tests/quickshare.rs is Sukkula to Sukkula plus a hand-built hostile sender. LocalSend is covered (localsend_loopback.rs:497, 589).
kept.failure_scenario: A change to wormhole/wire.rs that breaks interop with the Python client (the directory offer, the transit ack format) passes CI. It is caught only if someone runs M-40, M-41 or M-42 on hardware.
kept.suggested_fix: Add a CI job that installs a pinned Python magic-wormhole and runs `cargo test --test wormhole_interop -- --ignored`. Add an rquickshare or known-good Quick Share peer loopback test, or record the gap in the spec.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute the gap itself. The failure scenario, though, is overstated for wormhole.

What checks out:
- docs/SPEC.md:169 (§7, Adapters layer) asks for loopback tests from Sukkula to the reference client on the same host, naming LocalSend CLI, `wormhole` CLI and rquickshare, using cargo test (integration). docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md:11 says the `wormhole` CLI meant here is the Python one.
- All four tests in crates/sukkula-engine/tests/wormhole_interop.rs (lines 91, 121, 152, 186) are `#[ignore]` and need SUKKULA_PY_WORMHOLE. The file header says so: "Ignored by default, since CI has no Python client."
- Nothing ever runs them: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only `cargo test --workspace --locked` and the per-feature `cargo test -p sukkula-engine`, with no `--ignored`, no Python install and no SUKKULA_PY_WORMHOLE. The Makefile's `test` and `check` targets are the same.
- There is no rquickshare interop test anywhere:
  - crates/sukkula-engine/tests/quickshare.rs is Sukkula to Sukkula plus a hand-built hostile sender.
  - ci/rqs-lib-tests.sh runs third_party/rqs_lib's own tests on the patched copy, so it is patched library against patched library.
  - Sukkula's Quick Share adapter is itself open-quickshare's core_lib with 18 patches (docs/UPSTREAM-QUICKSHARE.md). Some patches touch the handshake, such as 0012 (P-256 decoding) and 0013 (MACs and schemes). A symmetric interop regression would pass Sukkula-to-Sukkula tests on both sides.
- Neither the spec nor the other docs record this gap as an accepted exception. So the rquickshare half is a plain deviation from §7.

What is overstated: a regression in wormhole/wire.rs that breaks the directory offer or the transit-ack format would not pass CI. These tests are not ignored and do run in CI:
- wire.rs:524 `our_messages_match_the_reference_shapes` pins the exact offer, file_ack and message_ack bytes and the transit_ack round trip. wire.rs:439 pins how a directory offer is parsed.
- tests/wormhole.rs:644 `a_zipped_directory_offer_is_saved_as_the_zip` drives a Python-style `{"offer":{"directory":{... "mode":"zipfile/deflated"}}}` offer end to end and checks both `file_ack` and the final `{"ack":"ok"}`.
- tests/wormhole.rs:716 and 738 cover Python-style text senders and receivers.
- tests/wormhole.rs:463, 564 and 603 interoperate with magic-wormhole's own Rust v1 implementation.

So on the wormhole side the uncovered risk is narrower than claimed: a misreading of the Python client's behaviour that the hand-written expectations share. It is not an ordinary regression in wire.rs.

It is still a real §7 test-coverage gap, mostly because Quick Share has no reference-client test at all. It affects no runtime behaviour and the manual checklist partly covers it, so low severity is right.

refuted.title: 'Offer::validate is the only way to an Offer' and consent-before-write are not enforced by types, although SECURITY.md says they are
refuted.why:
The facts in the claim are accurate. Offer and OfferFile (crates/sukkula-core/src/offer.rs:96-125) have only pub fields. Ctx::inbox() is pub (crates/sukkula-engine/src/ctx.rs:136-140). Ctx::begin_file (ctx.rs:262-273) takes any &TransferHandle and &OfferFile. But this is not a defect under the spec, and the claim's main premise misreads SECURITY.md.

1. SECURITY.md never says S2, S4 or S5 are enforced by the type system. The only type-system claim is the 'One writer' bullet: 'a received file can only be created from a SafeName'. That holds: SafeName(String) has a private field (name.rs:40), and Inbox::begin requires &SafeName. The claim concedes this. The 'Where each guarantee is checked' table defines what 'enforced in the code and checked in CI' means for these rules, and it names tests and fuzzers, not types:
   - S2: text.rs tests, properties display_keeps_its_promises, fuzz text_display.
   - S4/S6: offer.rs tests, validate_never_passes_a_bad_offer, fuzz offer_validate, the hostile suites.
   - S5: consent.rs tests, localsend_loopback::a_declined_offer_writes_nothing, wormhole::a_declined_offer_moves_no_data_and_leaves_no_file, localsend_hostile::uploads_without_consent_or_the_right_token_are_refused_unread.
   All of these exist.

2. The consent bullet is a statement about adapter behaviour: 'No adapter reads a payload before Ctx::offer returns an accepted offer.' It says nothing about types, and it is true of the code:
   - Ctx::inbox() has no callers in any adapter; grep finds none.
   - begin_file is called only from localsend/server.rs:892, quickshare/receive.rs:373 and wormhole/receive.rs:297. All three are on the accepted path.
   - begin_views is used only for sends and the busy test.

3. 'Offer::validate is the only way to an Offer' describes how data flows through the code as written, and it is true. Every Offer in the repo comes from validate, including the test helpers in consent.rs:288 and properties.rs:546. The only struct literal is inside validate itself (offer.rs:234, 273). The claim concedes this.

4. The failure scenario is a hypothetical future bug in adapter code, not something the current code can do. Even that bug is partly contained today:
   - Inbox::begin checks size > MAX_FILE_BYTES itself (inbox.rs:203).
   - Every file is still named by a SafeName and written into the inbox staging directory.
   - Ctx::inbox() could simply be removed, and the S5 tests for each adapter would catch a pre-consent write on the tested paths.

What remains is a hardening suggestion: private fields, or begin_file taking an &Accepted, would turn a tested convention into a compile-time fact. The doc could also be read as overclaiming. That is worth doing but is not a present defect or a spec violation. If it is kept at all, it is low or informational, as claimed.

refuted.title: Every UDP datagram to port 53317, from any source, is parsed before the S7 check
refuted.why:
The facts in the claim are right, but they don't add up to a defect under the spec, and the failure scenario doesn't work.

What is true: upstream `multicast::start` (packages/core/src/multicast/socket.rs:105) binds 0.0.0.0:53317 with SO_REUSEPORT once per interface address, using `InterfaceFilter::default()`. So a unicast datagram that reaches the phone on any interface goes into `receive_loop`. That loop runs `serde_json::from_slice::<MulticastMessageV2>` on it (mod.rs:367) before Sukkula's `screen` sees the source. The module doc in reach.rs:6-8 says such a peer "is dropped before a byte of it is parsed", which is wrong for this path.

Why it is refuted:
1. Not a violation of the spec. SPEC.md:119 defines S7 as "Only private, link-local or ULA addresses are **answered**". SECURITY.md:37-38 puts in scope "A LAN protocol **answering** a peer outside ...". `screen` (discovery.rs:163-186) runs `permits` before anything is sent or kept, and the test `announcements_are_screened_before_anything_is_sent` checks 8.8.8.8, 100.64.1.1 and v4-mapped public addresses. Nothing is answered, stored or connected to.
2. The behaviour is already stated at the cited line. discovery.rs:160-162 says: "The datagram has been parsed by upstream by now -- at most 64 KiB of JSON, the only thing read before this check; nothing is sent and nothing is kept." The parse uses one fixed 64 KiB buffer per socket that is reused for every datagram. Memory and CPU per datagram are bounded, so the SECURITY.md clause on unbounded resource use does not apply.
3. The denial-of-service scenario does not hold:
   - For an unpermitted source, `consume` (discovery.rs:206-239) does one atomic load (`receiving()` or `discovering()`), `canonical`, and a range check in `ReachPolicy::permits`, then `continue`. That is far cheaper than each producer iteration, which is a recvfrom syscall plus a JSON parse, so the 16-slot queue drains faster than it fills. Off-LAN traffic cannot keep it full or stall `event_tx.send().await` for the Wi-Fi loop.
   - LAN multicast is delivered to every socket bound to the port, so it does not depend on the one reuseport socket the attacker's unicast hashes to.
   - The real cost of a flood is receiving the packets. The suggested fix (recv, then check the source before parsing) would still pay that cost.
   - A LAN attacker, which is in scope anyway, can do the same with permitted addresses.
   - The scenario also depends on the carrier and connman letting unsolicited inbound UDP through, which the claim itself concedes.
4. The reach.rs sentence is not a guarantee only this path breaks. It is a loose description that already fails for Quick Share discovery: mdns-sd 0.21.4 binds INADDR_ANY:5353 (service_daemon.rs:861/1262) and parses DNS packets from any source before patch 0016's AddrFilter applies. It describes connection-level peers, where the check does run before the handshake or read (localsend/server.rs:305, quickshare/receive.rs:114).

Residual: at most a documentation nit. reach.rs:6-8 should say that discovery datagrams are parsed, bounded, by the upstream libraries before the policy runs, and are never answered. No security or availability impact.

refuted.title: One or a few LAN addresses can fill the 64-peer table and keep later real peers off the Send list
refuted.why:
The mechanics are accurate. `upsert` (peers.rs:82) refuses a new fingerprint once the table holds 64 entries. `allow_discovery` gives each address 8 sightings per 10 s, which is 80 per 100 s TTL, enough for one address to keep 64 entries alive. Any self-signed certificate is accepted. So a LAN attacker can fill the table and keep later peers out. I still refute it as a defect, for these reasons:

1. **This is the documented design, and a test pins it.** The peers.rs module doc (lines 5-7) says: "When the table is full a new peer is not admitted until a stale one expires: evicting on arrival would let a flood of fresh certificates push out the phone the user is about to send to." The test `the_table_is_bounded_and_keeps_who_it_has` checks exactly this. Quick Share's table (quickshare/discovery.rs:160) follows the same rule. The claim describes the downside of a trade-off the code chose on purpose; the code does what it says it does.

2. **The suggested fix does not hold against the threat model.** SECURITY.md and mod.rs L6 assume a LAN attacker has "as many addresses as it wants". With a quota of 2 per address, 32 addresses fill 64 slots, all within quota. Evicting the stalest entry brings back the flood attack the module doc names: the attacker refreshes its own entries constantly, so the real peer, heard only on the 30 s announce cycle, is the stalest and gets pushed out. Any bounded table facing an attacker with unlimited addresses and certificates can be denied one way or the other. The code picked "keep who you have".

3. **This is not UI spoofing as the spec and SECURITY.md define it.** S2 and SECURITY.md's "Spoofing in the UI" cover text that displays as something it is not: bidi overrides, invisible characters, combining floods, rich text. An attacker announcing the plain alias "Liisa's Pixel" is the LocalSend protocol's own weakness: aliases are self-declared and unauthenticated. SECURITY.md lists protocol weaknesses as out of scope. The impersonation works without filling the table (two "Liisa's Pixel" rows). Filling it only hides the real one, which is a denial of discovery. SECURITY.md's in-scope denial-of-service is crash, hang or unbounded resources, and the table is bounded as S6 and "Bounded everything" require.

4. **Discovery can already be denied more cheaply.** Only `MAX_ANSWERS` = 4 answers are in flight at once, each allowed up to 3 s (`ANSWER_TIMEOUT`), and "announcements beyond are ignored" (discovery.rs:38-42, 225-227). A couple of addresses answering slowly keep all four slots busy and Liisa's announcement is dropped, with no need to fill the table. So the table policy gives an attacker nothing it does not already have.

5. **The scenario has one factual error.** In "Send via…"-only mode Receive is off, so the HTTPS server is not running, and `register` returns 403 "Not receiving" even when it is (server.rs:449-451). The attacker cannot "register 64 certificates". It would have to use the announcement-answer path, which works, so this weakens the scenario without breaking it.

At most this belongs as a documentation note under SECURITY.md's "Known limitations", next to the consent-slot denial-of-service. If it is treated as real, severity stays low.

refuted.title: Any LAN host can take over a listed Quick Share peer by reusing its endpoint id, and the sender never shows the PIN, so the redirect is undetectable
refuted.why:
The mechanics in the claim are accurate, but the result is not a defect under the spec and SECURITY.md, and the extra capability it describes is marginal.

What checks out:
- discovery.rs:163 keys peers by `qs:<endpoint id>` only, and `insert` overwrites the stored address.
- rqs_lib `parse_mdns_name` (third_party/rqs_lib/src/utils.rs) ignores the last two bytes. mdns_discovery.rs caches by fullname, so an attacker's instance name that differs only in those bytes gets its own cache slot but maps to the same Sukkula row.
- `OutboundRequest::pin_code()` is never read on the send side (send.rs), and no QML page shows a PIN for outgoing transfers. The only PIN in QML is `consentPin` in the consent dialog.

Why it is refuted:
1. It is not a rule violation. SECURITY.md defines "Spoofing in the UI" narrowly: a name, alias, model or message that displays as something it is not through bidi overrides, invisible characters or combining-mark floods, or that is rendered as rich text or a link. Copying another device's plain visible name is not in that class, and S2 is not meant to stop it.
2. F-QS3 does not cover the send side. SPEC §4 says "Show the 4-digit PIN from the handshake in the consent dialog", which is the receive path. receive.rs puts `ir.pin_code()` into the offer, and tst_consent.qml checks it. No F- requirement asks for a PIN on send.
3. SECURITY.md puts it out of scope, and on purpose. The only in-scope rule about a send reaching the wrong peer is LocalSend's F-LS3, where a certificate fingerprint exists to pin to. There is deliberately no Quick Share equivalent. "Weaknesses in the protocols themselves (... Quick Share ...)" are listed as out of scope. In Everyone mode, Quick Share LAN discovery is unauthenticated: the endpoint id is 4 bytes the peer chooses, and the name and device type come from the peer's own `n` record.
4. Reusing the endpoint id is not needed for the attack. Any LAN host can announce the same name and phone icon under a fresh endpoint id and get a row that looks identical, and the user cannot tell which one is real. The attacker can also announce while the real Pixel is not announcing, since Android only advertises while its share sheet is open or after a BLE nudge. Reusing the id only merges the duplicate row. The suggested "key by instance name plus address, or show a conflict" leaves the attack open: the attacker uses a new id and the user sees two identical "Pixel" rows.
5. The suggested sender-side PIN would not stop the leak. A Quick Share sender does not wait for any PIN confirmation. send.rs starts sending as soon as the receiver sends `Accepted`, which a substitute receiver does at once. Android behaves the same way. At best the PIN would reveal the swap after the data has gone. In a pure substitution (no relay to the real Pixel), the Pixel's screen shows no request and no PIN at all, which is the same thing the user could already notice.

At most this is a low-severity hardening note (last-writer-wins on an endpoint id makes a copied name slightly stealthier), not the claimed medium-severity spoofing defect. | The code does what the claim says. discovery.rs:163 overwrites by_id["qs:<id>"] with whatever announcement arrived last. rqs_lib's parse_mdns_name (utils.rs:104) ignores the last two bytes, so a second instance name gets its own cache slot in mdns_discovery.rs but lands on the same Sukkula row. send.rs never reads OutboundRequest::pin_code(), and no event or QML page shows a PIN for outgoing sends. Even so, this is not a defect under the project's spec or security policy, and the claimed impact does not hold up:

1. **No spec requirement is broken.** F-QS3 asks for the handshake PIN "in the consent dialog", which is the receive side. FFI.md says the offer_pending `pin` is "to compare with the sender's screen", so the PIN exists for the receiving user. Nothing in the spec requires Quick Share to authenticate who you send to. LocalSend has such a rule (F-LS3), and SECURITY.md lists "a LocalSend send reaching a peer other than the one ... announced" as in scope. It lists no Quick Share equivalent, which reads as a deliberate choice.

2. **This is not "Spoofing in the UI" as SECURITY.md defines it.** That rule covers text that displays as something it is not: bidi overrides, invisible characters, mark floods, rich text or links. An attacker choosing the alias "Pixel 9" is a name the peer asserts about itself, shown faithfully. In Everyone mode a Quick Share name has no authentication, and "weaknesses in the protocols themselves (... Quick Share ...)" are explicitly out of scope.

3. **The endpoint-id keying does not create the attack.** mDNS has no source authentication. mdns-sd 0.21.4 (dns_parser.rs ~2420) accepts TTL-0 goodbyes from any host and expires the record a second later. So an attacker can remove the real row and announce its own "Pixel 9" under any endpoint id, or reuse the exact instance name. The suggested fix of keying by instance name plus address would only produce two identical-looking "Pixel 9" rows. The user still cannot tell them apart.

4. **Showing a PIN to the sender would not stop the leak.** Quick Share has no confirmation step on the sending side. In send.rs::session, once the receiver sends Accepted, send_file streams at once. A rogue receiver accepts immediately, and the files are gone before anyone could compare PINs. The PIN comparison protects the receiver's decision, not the sender's confidentiality. So "the one check Quick Share gives against a substituted receiver" gives the sender no such protection. The redirect is also not undetectable: the real Pixel never shows an incoming dialog.

At most this is a hardening idea: warn when a listed peer's address changes, and show the PIN when sending, to match Android. It is not a security or spec defect as claimed. If kept at all, it should be low severity.

refuted.title: Discovery can be saturated: 64 fake services fill rqs_lib's cache and Sukkula's peer table, and real devices are never listed
refuted.why:
The mechanics in the claim are accurate, but under the project's own spec and security policy this is not a defect.

What checks out:
- In third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns_discovery.rs:93-97, a new fullname is skipped once the cache holds 64 entries. An entry leaves only on a ServiceRemoved.
- mdns-sd 0.21.4 does not cap the TTL of normal responses, so a sender's long TTL keeps its record alive.
- In crates/sukkula-engine/src/quickshare/discovery.rs:160, insert() returns None once MAX_PEERS is reached.
- allow_discovery is keyed by the announced IP.
So a persistent LAN host announcing 64 valid services can keep newly arriving real devices out of the list.

Why it is refuted:
1. It is outside what SECURITY.md counts as a vulnerability. The only peer-triggered DoS in scope is "a crash, hang, or unbounded memory, CPU or descriptor use." This case is bounded by design. The spec's section 5 goals are no writes outside the inbox, consent, no crash or memory exhaustion, and no UI spoofing. None of them is breached.
2. S7 does not cover it. S7 says: "Only private, link-local or ULA addresses are answered on the LAN protocols; discovery replies are rate-limited per IP." That rule is about reach and our replies, not about keeping the discovery list available. "S7 (bounded DoS)" misreads the rule.
3. Refusing new entries rather than evicting is deliberate, documented and tested:
   - The cap is the upstream fix for R12 ("memory grows with announcements", Patch 0016).
   - localsend/peers.rs states the policy: "When the table is full a new peer is not admitted ... evicting on arrival would let a flood of fresh certificates push out the phone the user is about to send to."
   - tests/quickshare.rs peers_are_bounded_and_reported asserts exactly this behaviour.
4. A LAN attacker can deny Quick Share discovery through the protocol itself, whatever the cache policy. mDNS is unauthenticated. mdns-sd turns a TTL-0 goodbye into a 1 s TTL (dns_parser.rs:2420), then expires the PTR and emits ServiceRemoved (service_daemon.rs:3065-3085). An attacker who sees a real phone's announcement can remove it, or spoof its instance name. SECURITY.md lists "weaknesses in the protocols themselves" as out of scope. The cap gives the attacker no ability it did not already have.
5. The suggested fix would not bound the attack:
   - Eviction by age or least-recent refresh lets a continuous flood of fresh fullnames push out real peers. That is the very reason peers.rs rejects eviction.
   - A cap per announced address fails because the reach filter accepts any private or link-local address, not only the local subnet, so 64 distinct addresses are trivial.
   - A cap per source fails because the source of a multicast packet on the LAN can be spoofed.

At most this is a gap in the documentation: discovery saturation could be listed next to the consent-slot DoS under "Known limitations". If it were treated as real, its severity would be low, not medium. | The code does what the claim says, but the behaviour is a deliberate, documented and tested design choice. The spec does not treat it as a defect.

What the claim gets right:
- rqs_lib skips a new fullname once 64 services are cached (third_party/rqs_lib/src/hdl/mdns_discovery.rs:93-97).
- Sukkula's `discovery::insert` refuses a new id once MAX_PEERS is reached (crates/sukkula-engine/src/quickshare/discovery.rs:160-162).
- mdns-sd 0.21.4 does not cap a received TTL. Only the legacy-unicast answer path caps TTLs.

Why it is still not a defect:
1. **The project chose refuse-when-full on purpose, and rejected the suggested fix.** The LocalSend peers table uses the same policy, and its module doc gives the reason (crates/sukkula-engine/src/localsend/peers.rs:5-7): "When the table is full a new peer is not admitted until a stale one expires: evicting on arrival would let a flood of fresh certificates push out the phone the user is about to send to." A test asserts this behaviour for Quick Share: crates/sukkula-engine/tests/quickshare.rs `peers_are_bounded_and_reported` checks that exactly MAX_PEERS of MAX_PEERS+10 are admitted. localsend/peers.rs has a matching test.
2. **The suggested fixes would not stop this attacker.**
   - Age or LRU eviction lets an attacker who keeps sending new fullnames push out the real phone.
   - A per-announced-address cap fails because the attacker picks the A records freely. Nothing probes them, so it can name 64 different private addresses.
   - A per-source cap has nothing to key on: rqs_lib's ServiceInfo carries no packet source address, and multicast sources on a LAN can be spoofed anyway.

   Under the claim's own condition, "for as long as the attacker keeps announcing", any bounded table can be starved. That is a property of unauthenticated mDNS discovery, which SECURITY.md lists as out of scope ("Weaknesses in the protocols themselves").
3. **The spec does not cover it.**
   - The goals in spec §5 are: no writes outside the inbox, nothing accepted without consent, no crash or memory exhaustion, no spoofing.
   - SECURITY.md's in-scope DoS is "a crash, hang, or unbounded memory, CPU or descriptor use". A full peer list is none of these, and the process stays responsive.
   - The cited rule, S7, requires only private addresses and per-IP rate limiting of discovery replies. Both hold: the filter is applied in rqs_lib, `allow_discovery` again in `found_or_lost`, and `permits` in `insert`. S7 promises nothing about the table's contents under a flood.
   - "Bounded everything" in SECURITY.md requires the hard peer cap that causes this behaviour. SECURITY.md lists a sibling LAN-availability trade-off, the two consent slots, as a known limitation.
4. **The retention detail changes attacker effort, not the outcome.** A sender-chosen TTL keeps entries only for one discovery session. Each `start()` drains Sukkula's table and builds a new MDnsDiscovery, with a new daemon and an empty cache. The failure scenario already assumes the attacker keeps announcing, so capping the TTL would not change the outcome either.

refuted.title: A Quick Share text is accepted on a sender-chosen title; the delivered text is never held to the introduced size or content
refuted.why:
The claim rests on the idea that the consent dialog shows the sender's text_title ("Lunch at 12?") or a size of 12. It shows neither.

1. **The dialog never shows the preview or its size.** raw_offer (crates/sukkula-engine/src/quickshare/receive.rs:232) does copy a truncated title into RawOffer.text. Offer::validate cleans it into Offer.text. But hub.rs:756 only turns it into `has_text: offer.text.is_some()`. OfferView (api.rs:418) has no text field, only `has_text: bool`. FFI.md's offer_pending examples match this. In qml/pages/ConsentDialog.qml:192-201, the only text-related item is the fixed label "Includes a text message.", shown when hasText is true. The dialog shows no text size either: total_bytes counts files only. Nothing else in the engine reads the Quick Share preview (checked with grep: only has_text, a log field in ctx.rs:206, and the LocalSend and wormhole paths use their own offers). So the user never sees "Lunch at 12?" and never agrees to any particular content or size.

2. **What the user accepts is simply "a text message from this sender",** with the sender's name and the Quick Share PIN (F-QS3). A 64 KiB text with a phishing URL, sent afterwards on the same connection by that same sender, is exactly what was consented to. Nothing on screen claimed otherwise.

refuted.title: obexd resolves a /proc/self path to itself, so a size-0 procfs file sends obexd's own process data
refuted.why:
The mechanism described is roughly accurate. check_file (hub.rs:1425) and source_path (obex.rs:289) only stat the path. A /proc/self file is a regular file of size 0, so it passes both checks. obexd then opens the same string in its own process and its put producer reads until EOF. Nothing in Sukkula stops that, and the Transferred > size abort (obex.rs:463) only runs after data has gone.

It is still not a defect under this project's spec and threat model:

1. **Who the attacker is.** SPEC §5 names the attacker as "anyone on the same Wi-Fi, within Bluetooth range, or holding a wormhole code". A peer has no route to the outgoing path. That path comes only from a `send` command built by Sukkula's own shell: the in-process FilePicker (qml/pages/FilePicker.qml) or the system Share menu (qml/share/ShareTarget.qml). Received files cannot put a /proc path into a send either: S1 sanitises their names and the inbox never creates links.

2. **The claim's own trigger is out of scope.** The trigger is "a hostile UI command". That means either Sukkula's own UI code is hostile, or another app shares a /proc path through the Share menu. Both need code already running as the phone's user. SECURITY.md lists "Attacks that need code already running as the phone's user" as out of scope.

3. **The module already documents this weakness.** The obex.rs module docs (lines 28-39) say "What obexd reads is not what the hub checked", and that obexd opens the file "outside Sukkula's sandbox". They say "the threat model here is peers in radio range, who cannot touch the path at all", and that the size and Transferred checks only narrow the gap. The "cancels one whose Transferred grows past it" wording admits that bytes past `size` can go out before the cancel. So the "sends at most size bytes" line in adapter.rs is best-effort for Bluetooth, and that is written down. The SECURITY.md known limitation "Bluetooth sends name a path... Remote peers cannot reach this" covers the same ground. The /proc/self case differs only in needing no race, and it still needs a hostile path source that runs as the user.

4. **The data only goes where the user sends it.** Even with a hostile sharer, nothing is sent until the user picks Bluetooth and one of their own paired devices on the Send page and confirms. The bytes go to that device, not to an attacker. If the user picks such a path themselves, they are sending their own session's process data to their own device.

5. **S8 is not the rule at stake.** S8 is about spawning processes and opening URLs or files in other apps, which is not what happens here.

Refusing /proc, /sys and /dev paths, or procfs-backed files, would be reasonable defence in depth. It does not fix a vulnerability under the spec.

refuted.title: sukkula_stop returns immediately while another stop of the same engine is still running, breaking 'after return, userdata may be freed'
refuted.why:
The code does what the claim says: lib.rs:379 takes the handle out of the registry before it stops the engine, so a second sukkula_stop on the same handle finds nothing and returns at once. But none of the three sub-scenarios breaks the documented contract.

1. hub.rs:1177-1180, stopping engine X from engine Y's callback. The header says "The callback must not call sukkula_stop()". FFI.md also documents the behaviour: "Stopping *another* engine from a callback waits for that engine's callback at most 3 seconds, since the two could be waiting for each other." Because that stop runs on a delivery thread, shutdown_logged picks Finish::Discard, so X's queued events are dropped rather than drained. This is forbidden use, and its outcome is documented.

2. The "header's own tolerated case", where the callback and another thread both stop the engine. Stopping from the callback is forbidden.
   - If the callback's stop wins the registry: all its work runs on the delivery thread while that thread is inside the sink. Engine::stop -> shutdown_logged -> delivery.is_current() -> finish(Discard) -> gate.close(Discard) closes the gate before the callback returns. No drain happens and the callback is never entered again; Gate::run sees Closed and exits. The claimed failure (a drain calling the callback with freed userdata) cannot happen here. The only thing still running is the forbidden in-progress call, which the header covers: "not called again once the current call returns".
   - If thread A's stop wins: A drains and joins normally. The early return belongs to the callback, which is still running and would not free its own userdata.

3. Two ordinary threads racing to stop the same handle. The spec does not support this usage.
   - The header and FFI.md sanction only "a command racing a stop on another thread" as harmless. They define sukkula_stop on "a handle already stopped" as ignored, and FFI.md says it is "refused like NULL rather than used". A stop on a NULL handle is a no-op, so the promise about returning cannot apply to it.
   - From the moment of registry removal the ABI already treats the handle as stopped: sukkula_command returns SUKKULA_ERR_NULL, which the header defines as "the engine was stopped". A later stop is therefore on a stopped handle and is ignored, as documented. The header also says "The handle is invalid afterwards".
   - The failure needs a shell in which one thread stops the engine without owning userdata while another thread concurrently stops it and frees userdata. That is a shell ownership bug of the same kind as destroying one handle twice: if both callers freed userdata, it would be a double free whatever the engine did.
   - The ffi tests and SECURITY.md cover only stale handles, stopping from the callback, and command hammering during a stop. Nothing in the spec promises that concurrent stops of one handle are serialised.
   - The real shell (src/bridge.cpp Bridge::stop) clears m_engine and stops on one thread, as the claim concedes, so nothing in the codebase reaches this path.

At most, the wording "a handle already stopped" could spell out that it includes a handle whose stop is still in progress. That is a documentation-precision nit, not a defect in the ABI's guarantee.

refuted.title: Send paths are accepted verbatim and followed through symlinks, including into Sukkula's own data directory (TLS key, PIN)

The code does what the claim says, but the failure scenario falls outside the threat model the project wrote down, so under the spec it is not a defect.

- `check_file` (crates/sukkula-engine/src/hub.rs:1425-1451) uses `tokio::fs::metadata`, which follows symlinks. The comment there says this is on purpose, because the picker hands out links. It only requires a regular file, and it takes the name from the link's own last path segment.
- Nothing refuses the data dir. The key is `localsend-key.pem` (localsend/identity.rs:28), not `key.pem`.
- The "Outside Downloads" label (SendPage.qml:238-267) only checks the path prefix. Its comment shows it is a hint about whether the sandbox lets Sukkula read the file, not a security check, so bypassing it with a link defeats nothing.

1. The scenario starts with "Another app with the Downloads permission creates ~/Downloads/holiday.jpg as a symlink". That is local code running under the phone user's UID: Harbour apps under Sailjail all run as the same user and are separated only by namespaces. docs/SECURITY.md lists "Attacks that need code already running as the phone's user" as out of scope. The Bluetooth known limitation says the same thing: another process of the same user swapping a send path is accepted, and "Remote peers cannot reach this."
2. In the spec, the attacker is a network, Bluetooth or wormhole peer (spec §5; SECURITY.md: "every byte, name, size and alias they send is treated as hostile"). Files the user picks from local storage are not treated as hostile input anywhere in the spec. The reviewer's premise "treating files on disk as hostile" is not in the threat model.
3. A remote peer cannot plant the link. The inbox only creates regular files: `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` in staging, then `linkat` of that file under a fresh name, never creating a symlink (S3). Wormhole folders arrive as an unopened .zip (F-MW3). So the only route to a symlink in ~/Downloads is local code or a user-driven tool, both outside Sukkula's responsibility.

A defence-in-depth change would still be reasonable: refuse sends that resolve inside `data_dir`, since `hub.rs` already has `resolved()` and `apart()`. The closest thing to a route without local attacker code is the user extracting a hostile archive containing a symlink with some other tool and then sending the result. That is speculative and depends on the user and third-party tools, not on Sukkula. If this is judged in scope anyway, the severity should stay low.

refuted.title: The RPM validator judges only the lexically last RPM, while the release publishes every device RPM
refuted.why:
The claim's failure scenario says a device RPM goes out unvalidated, but the pipeline fails closed, so that cannot happen.

1. The sort part of the claim is correct. I checked it with both the default and C.UTF-8 locales. `sort | tail -1` at .github/workflows/rpm.yml:222 does pick RPMS/harbour-sukkula-extras-0.1.0-1.aarch64.rpm over RPMS/harbour-sukkula-0.1.0-1.aarch64.rpm, because the main package's version starts with a digit and digits sort before letters. So any realistic subpackage (`%package extras` or `%package -n harbour-sukkula-<word>`) is the one chosen, not the main package.

2. The chosen RPM then goes to `./scripts/build-rpm.sh check "$rpm" "$ROOTFS"`. `check()` (scripts/build-rpm.sh:169-187) always unpacks the RPM and runs `ci/check-elf.sh ... "$unpack/usr/bin/$NAME"` with NAME=harbour-sukkula. In the claim's scenario the binary is in the main package, so the extras RPM has no /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula. check-elf.sh:51 (`[[ -r "$elf" ]] || { echo "check-elf: FAIL $elf is not readable"; exit 1; }`) then fails, `check` returns 1, and the "Validate the RPM" step fails. harbour-validate-rpm.sh would also run on the extras package, which has no .desktop file, no binary and data outside /usr/share/<its own name>, so it would be rejected there too.

3. The release job has `needs: rpm`, and its `if:` has no status function, so GitHub adds `success()`. A red validation step means nothing is gathered or published, and no release notes claiming validation are written. The claimed outcome ("Both are published with release notes claiming validation") cannot occur.

4. A subpackage would be skipped only if its name sorted before `harbour-sukkula-<digit>` (e.g. `harbour-sukkula-0x`), or if it also carried /usr/bin/harbour-sukkula as a duplicated file. Both are contrived, and nothing in the spec or docs points that way. Today rpm/harbour-sukkula.spec has no `%package`, and debuginfo is off (`%global debug_package %{nil}`).

What remains is at most a clarity nit: adding a subpackage would show up as a confusing check-elf "not readable" failure instead of a clear "more than one device RPM" error. The build still stops, so this is not a defect under the spec (§7: every published package passes the validator).

refuted.title: No scheduled deep fuzzing and no corpus caching, minimisation or fold-back: every run restarts from the same few seeds and throws away what it found

The facts in the claim are correct. ci.yml:10-14 has no `schedule` trigger. `fuzz-smoke` (ci.yml:147-185) runs `scripts/fuzz-smoke.sh 60` over an empty `fuzz/corpus` plus `fuzz/seeds`. Its rust-cache caches only the build. It uploads `fuzz/artifacts` only on failure. `/fuzz/corpus/` is gitignored. The untracked local corpus has only the eight core targets (command_json 1733, start_config 1099, settings_json 1736, and so on).

It is still not a defect under Sukkula's spec. It is a request to copy a design choice from a sibling project.

1. **The spec names this exact gate.** SPEC.md §7 line 164 says: "A change merges only when CI passes: ... a 60-second fuzz smoke run". The table row the claim cites (line 171) asks for "cargo-fuzz, corpus in repo" for the parsers. Both are met:
   - Every target, including all eight protocol-parser targets, runs 60 s per pull request.
   - The corpus is in the repo: `fuzz/seeds/<t>`, 4-18 inputs per target, with dictionaries.
   
   Nothing in SPEC.md, SECURITY.md or BUILDING.md asks for scheduled or nightly fuzzing, a cached corpus, or automatic fold-back. SECURITY.md:181 and :196 describe the same thing: "60 s each per pull request", "committed seeds".
2. **Deeper fuzzing and fold-back are documented as manual, on purpose.**
   - fuzz/README.md's layer table: "60 s per target in CI, longer by hand".
   - fuzz/README.md "A finding": "Worthwhile corpus growth can be folded into `fuzz/seeds/<target>/` after `cargo fuzz cmin`, keeping the committed seed small and reviewable."
   - fuzz/README.md explains why `fuzz/corpus` is gitignored: libFuzzer writes to it and only reads the committed seeds.

3. **"Gate with a hole" does not fit.** A nightly scheduled job does not gate merges, so adding one would not close a hole in the gate. Clove's own comment says its fuzz job "runs on a schedule rather than blocking every push". That is a different project with a different spec that made the opposite trade-off, so it cannot be used as the standard here.
4. **The "stuck at shallow depth" scenario is partly addressed by how the seeds are built.**
   - The Quick Share seeds are generated from scripts in `fuzz/src/seeds.rs` to reach every state, including the whole handshake to a received file.
   - `cargo test --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --lib` runs in the same CI job and checks that each seed still reaches its milestone. So the multi-frame states in the failure scenario are covered from the first second.
   - The README records longer manual runs of the protocol targets: the two Quick Share targets for 180 s more, with grown corpora.

A step for longer runs and fold-back therefore exists. It is manual and not scheduled.

4. Clove is the benchmark the claim uses, and SECURITY.md lists what Sukkula takes from it. The list says "fuzz targets with dictionaries and committed seeds". It does not mention nightly or scheduled fuzzing. Sukkula also makes the fuzz smoke block every pull request, which clove does not; clove's fuzz job runs only on its schedule or a manual dispatch. Missing nightly fuzzing does not break any stated guarantee.

5. The failure scenario is only a general point: a bug deeper than 60 s from the seeds would not be found in CI. That is true of any time-limited gate, and the spec accepts it by choosing 60 s. No actual defect in the Quick Share, wormhole or LocalSend parsers is shown. The README also records longer runs by hand, including an extra 180 s on the two Quick Share targets, and says those corpora reached every milestone the harness records. So "no target ever gets more than 60 s of search depth" is not accurate either.

Adding a scheduled job with corpus caching and `cmin` would be reasonable hardening. As a finding against the spec it does not hold. If it were kept anyway, it would be low severity, as a process improvement.

refuted.title: No lock per directory: a second engine's Inbox::open sweeps and deletes a running engine's in-flight staging files
refuted.why:
The code does what the claim says. There is no flock anywhere in crates/. Inbox::with (inbox.rs:153-157) always runs sweep_stale, and that unlinks every regular *.part in the staging directory. If a second engine really did open the same directory, the first engine's place() would fail at the statat at inbox.rs:423 and the transfer would fail. The claim fails on its premise and on the rule it cites.

1. The rule is not Sukkula's. "One daemon per data directory" is in /home/user/muhnschein/clove/SECURITY.md:125, for clove's daemon and its control socket. Sukkula's SPEC.md and SECURITY.md never mention it. The "Compared with clove" section of SECURITY.md lists exactly what Sukkula took from clove, and this is not on the list. S3 still holds in the scenario: nothing outside the inbox is touched, nothing is overwritten, and the partial file is gone. The only result is an error on a transfer, which is safe.

2. The D-Bus path in step 2 cannot happen together with step 1. Engine.qml calls bridge.start() while the window is being built. The Loader for share/ShareTarget.qml is also in harbour-sukkula.qml. It is synchronous (no `asynchronous`), and its ShareProvider has `registerName: true`, so it claims sukkula.sukkula during that same load. Bridge sends engine events to QML through a queued invokeMethod. So no offer, consent dialog or accept can reach QML until the event loop runs, and by then the whole scene exists and the name is claimed. An in-flight .part (step 1) therefore means the first instance already owns sukkula.sukkula. The share sheet then reaches that instance and no second one is activated. The sweep runs only once per engine, at Inbox::open. A second instance activated early would sweep while the first could not yet have a staging file.

3. The only path left is a user starting a second copy by hand from a terminal. That bypasses the platform's single-instance launch (X-Nemo-Single-Instance=yes; the Qt shell's Bridge::start also refuses a second engine in one process). Such a copy also collides with the LocalSend listener on fixed port 53317 and with the D-Bus name. The spec asks for no engine-level lock against that. A user with a shell can also delete ~/Downloads/Sukkula/.partial directly.

The first-run key/certificate race heals itself. load() in localsend/identity.rs detects a mismatched pair ("tls::check_pair") and makes a new one at the next start. Each running engine holds a valid identity in memory.

Adding a lock would be a reasonable hardening step, but it is not a defect under Sukkula's spec on any supported launch path. If it were counted, low severity is right: it needs a deliberate manual double launch, and the only result is one failed transfer with no damage outside the inbox.

refuted.title: Sailjail confinement is asserted but never checked or reported at runtime
refuted.why:
This is not a defect under the spec. The claim treats a hardening idea from clove as a requirement that Sukkula never makes.

1. The guarantee says exactly what the code does. docs/SECURITY.md:147-148 reads: "Sailjail grants Internet;Bluetooth;Downloads and nothing else, and the Harbour gate fails on any other permission." That is a promise about the declared grant, and it names what enforces it. The table row at SECURITY.md:182 and the P.2 check in ci/harbour-check.sh (lines ~728-744, with its selftest) do enforce it. harbour-sukkula.desktop declares exactly those three permissions. No sentence in SPEC.md §2, SECURITY.md or HARBOUR.md promises runtime detection or reporting of confinement. The claim admits the guarantee is "checked only as a declaration", and that is all the guarantee says.

2. The clove comparison sets no requirement here. SECURITY.md's "Compared with clove" section lists what Sukkula shares with clove: the guarantee table, the mutation sweeps, the hostile suites, the linter and dependency bans, and text scrubbing. A runtime sandbox verdict is not in that list. Under "Where it differs" the doc says Sukkula has no seccomp or Landlock of its own and relies on Sailjail (firejail), "which already confines it". Confinement is handed to the OS on purpose. clove's sandbox.rs reports on confinement the daemon applies to itself; Sukkula applies none of its own, so there is nothing of its own to check.

3. The failure scenario is outside the threat model.
   - Starting the app from a developer-mode terminal without sailjail/invoker is the device owner choosing to run it unconfined.
   - An OS update changing the Sailjail profile is under the OS vendor's control, not the app's.
   - The harmful part, a symlink planted in ~/Downloads pointing at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, needs a local process running as the user. SECURITY.md lists "Attacks that need code already running as the phone's user" as out of scope.
   - Peers cannot create links: the inbox only links its own staged regular files into place.
   - The send path follows symlinks on purpose and says so (hub.rs check_file: "Follows symlinks on purpose: the picker hands out links"; the same comment is in localsend/send.rs and quickshare/send.rs).
   - The user still has to pick the file and send it.
   - The Bluetooth path already sends through obexd outside the sandbox. obex.rs and SECURITY.md accept that as a known limitation, for the same same-user-process reason.

4. The other claims that supposedly rely on runtime confinement are not security promises that fail open.
   - SECURITY.md:73 ("Files outside ~/Downloads may be unreadable") is a known functional limitation. Running unconfined only makes it less restrictive, and it breaks no guarantee.
   - The manual tests say to install from the release RPM, and tests/README.md says the app is started from the launcher and the Share menu. That is the Sailjail launch path. M-44's wording "inside Sailjail" explains why the test should pass; it is not a security assertion.

At most this is a hardening suggestion or feature request: add a runtime confinement verdict. It is not a spec or guarantee violation.

refuted.title: A send command can ship the LocalSend TLS private key (and the PIN file) to any peer
refuted.why:
The code does behave as described. `check_file` (crates/sukkula-engine/src/hub.rs:1425) accepts any absolute path to a regular file and follows symlinks. `ShareTarget.pathOf` and `SendPage.addFile` accept any path that starts with '/'. The key lives in data_dir as `localsend-key.pem` (localsend/identity.rs:28). But the scenario cannot happen with the attacker the project defends against, so this is not a defect under the spec.

1. **Out of the threat model.** SPEC §5 names the attacker as "anyone on the same Wi-Fi, within Bluetooth range, or holding a wormhole code". SECURITY.md lists "Attacks that need code already running as the phone's user" as out of scope. The scenario needs exactly that: another app, which on Sailfish runs as defaultuser even inside Sailjail, has to share a crafted resource. The symlink variant (a link planted in ~/Downloads) needs local code too. SECURITY.md already treats this class the same way for Bluetooth: "Another process of the same user could swap the path ... Remote peers cannot reach this."

2. **No remote route.** Only the UI issues send commands. A peer cannot put a path in a `send`. The inbox never creates links (S3), so a peer cannot plant a symlink in the download directory for a later send to follow.

3. **No rule treats the UI as hostile.** I found none in SPEC.md, SECURITY.md or FFI.md. FFI.md's "hostile commands" row covers robustness against malformed commands (no crash, bounded, replies after panics), not the shell as an adversary. The engine runs inside the Qt process through sukkula-ffi, so a hostile UI could read the key file itself. A check in `prepare` would add no boundary against it.

4. **The user chooses the send.** A share only fills the Send page. The page shows the basename ("localsend-key.pem"), and nothing is sent until the user picks a peer or makes a wormhole code. The system share sheet also needs the user to pick "Send nearby". FilePicker.qml says the browser shows "exactly what Sailjail lets Sukkula read", so the user could just as well pick the file there. Sending a file the user deliberately chose is the app's purpose, not the key "leaving" through an attack.

5. **S9 is not broken.** It says "The TLS key has mode 0600 and is never logged". Neither is violated. The SECURITY.md line "TLS private key leaving key.pem" sits in a list scoped by the threat model above.

A deny-list for data_dir would be reasonable defence in depth, but as a vulnerability it needs local code plus an explicit user send. The project explicitly puts that out of scope. | The code does what the claim says, but under the project's own threat model this is not a defect.

What the code does: `prepare`/`check_file` (crates/sukkula-engine/src/hub.rs:1389-1455) accept any absolute path to a readable regular file. They do not exclude `data_dir`, where the key lives (`localsend-key.pem`, crates/sukkula-engine/src/localsend/identity.rs:28). ShareTarget.qml `pathOf` and SendPage.qml `addFile` accept any path that starts with '/'.

Why it is still not a defect:
1. **The trigger is out of scope.** The failure scenario starts with "Another app shares a resource", which means a malicious app already running on the phone. docs/SECURITY.md lists "Attacks that need code already running as the phone's user" as out of scope. Sailjailed apps still run under the same user ID (defaultuser). The Known limitations section takes the same view elsewhere: for the Bluetooth path swap it says another same-user process could do it and "Remote peers cannot reach this", and accepts that.
2. **No peer input reaches this code.** The spec's attacker (SPEC §5) is someone on the same Wi-Fi, in Bluetooth range, or holding a wormhole code. The paths passed to `check_file` come only from the local UI: the Share menu or the in-process file picker. Nothing a peer sends can name a file to send, so none of the S-rules' peer-input guarantees are involved.
3. **The documented contract matches the code.** docs/FFI.md `send` says only: "Every file must be an absolute path to a regular file (`bad_file`) within the size limits". There is no rule that `data_dir` must be excluded from sends. S9 in the spec requires the key to be mode 0600 and never logged, and both still hold. I found no "owner's rule" in the repo that treats the UI or shell as hostile. FFI.md's "hostile commands" row covers robustness against malformed commands, not trust in the paths a command names.
4. **The user has to choose to send it.** The Send page lists the file by its basename, "localsend-key.pem". Nothing is sent until the user picks a recipient: a nearby peer, a paired Bluetooth device, or a wormhole code they read out. The attacker also has to be that recipient. The in-process file picker can browse the same directory anyway (FilePicker.qml: "shows exactly what Sailjail lets Sukkula read"), so a user can already choose to send this file on purpose.

Refusing paths inside `data_dir` in `check_file` would be reasonable defence in depth, so I would log it as low-severity hardening at most. It is not a medium-severity S9 violation.

refuted.title: The sukkula-core 90 % line-coverage requirement is not measured anywhere
refuted.why:
The facts in the claim are right, but the spec does not treat this as a defect, and the requirement it cites is already met.

1. **The facts check out.** No CI job, Makefile target or script runs cargo-llvm-cov or any other coverage tool. I searched the tree for `llvm-cov`, `coverage`, `tarpaulin`, `grcov` and `profraw`, leaving out `target/`, `third_party/` and `Cargo.lock`. The only hits are SPEC.md:175, fuzz/README.md (libFuzzer coverage) and a .gitignore entry. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and the Makefile `check` target have nothing on coverage.

2. **Coverage is not part of the §7 merge gate.** SPEC.md §7 lists exactly what CI must pass before a change merges: `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy -D warnings`, tests, `cargo deny`, the 60-second fuzz smoke run, the ARM cross-build and the Harbour gate. Line coverage is not on that list. It appears separately as a "Coverage target" line after the test-layer table. ci.yml says "The gate (spec §7)" and runs exactly the listed items, so CI matches the spec. The spec asks that `sukkula-core` reach 90 % measured with `cargo llvm-cov`. It does not ask CI to enforce it with `--fail-under-lines`.

3. **The requirement is met, by a wide margin.** cargo-llvm-cov and llvm-tools are installed here. I built the `sukkula-core` test binaries with `cargo llvm-cov` (target dir in the scratchpad). The one-command run failed in this sandbox: the hostile and properties test binaries were reported missing at exec time, though they were on disk afterwards. So I ran all three test binaries directly under LLVM_PROFILE_FILE and then ran `cargo llvm-cov report -p sukkula-core`. All tests passed: 106 unit, 9 hostile, 19 properties. Line coverage totals 98.41 % (2701 lines, 43 missed). By file:
   - inbox.rs 96.10 %
   - name.rs 99.57 %
   - offer.rs 100 %
   - store.rs 97.16 %
   - config.rs, hex.rs and reach.rs 100 %
   - consent.rs 99.44 %, dirfd.rs 97.58 %, text.rs 99.33 %

   The claim's line "the 90 % requirement can go unmet indefinitely" describes a possible future regression, not a present failure.

4. **Nothing else claims coverage is enforced.** SECURITY.md, BUILDING.md and the CI comments never say coverage is measured in CI. So this is not a gap between what the docs promise and what the code does.

What remains is a process improvement: a regression guard, such as adding `cargo llvm-cov -p sukkula-core --fail-under-lines 90` to CI, would stop the figure slipping unnoticed. It is not a breach of the spec, and nothing in the current tree fails the target. If a reviewer still wants it logged, it should be low severity, not medium. | The facts in the claim are right, but they don't show a defect under the spec.

What is true:
- ci.yml, the Makefile, ci/ and scripts/ never run cargo-llvm-cov or any other coverage tool.
- `git grep -i 'llvm-cov|coverage'` only finds SPEC.md:175 and unrelated fuzz and libFuzzer notes.
- No coverage figure is recorded in docs/.

Why it is not a defect under the spec:
1. The spec lists what CI must enforce, and coverage is not on the list. SPEC.md §7 names the merge gate in full: "A change merges only when CI passes: cargo fmt --check, clippy -D warnings, tests, cargo deny, a 60-second fuzz smoke run, the ARM cross-build, and the Harbour gate". The Makefile header says `make check` mirrors "exactly what CI's per-pull-request gate runs". ci.yml and the Makefile cover that list. The 90 % line is stated separately as a "Coverage target" on the crate. It is not a CI gate, so a missing CI job for it doesn't break §7. The suggested fix adds a gate the spec never asked for.
2. The target is met today. I ran `cargo llvm-cov -p sukkula-core --locked --summary-only`, with the target dir in my scratchpad so no repository file changed. All 134 tests passed (106 unit, 9 hostile, 19 property). Total line coverage is 98.45 % (2701 lines, 42 missed). The lowest file is inbox.rs at 96.10 %. Every other file is above 97 %.
3. The failure scenario is a hypothetical future change, not a present failure. Deleting half of inbox.rs's tests is not something the tree does now.
